subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock yesterday I was proceeding to narrate the difficulties of the ordinary member in his attempt to grasp the financial situation as presented in the budget speech of this year. The second budget speech, as delivered by the apparently second Acting Minister of Finance, (Mr. Marler) has left us in a position of great confusion. We got as far as the statement that the ordinary revenue of the country was $344,000,000 and the ordinary expenditure $342,000,000, leaving a supposed balance or surplus of $1,823,000 odd. But we ordinary members were nonplussed by this grant of cash of $18,027,000 to the Canadian National Railways. If we take that as ordinary expenditure, no matter where it has been obtained, we have a deficit of $16,204,000; but if we accept the conclusion as arrived at by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), and with which we in this section of the House agree, namely that all assistance to the railways, whether cash, guaranteed loan or unguaranteed loan, is to be taken as a debt of this country and should be so marked and should be included in our obligations, then we can without any further discussion and1 without any evasion say that our additions for the year to the national debt comprise the following items:

Cash to Canadian National Railways.. .. $ 18,027,000 Last year's vote to the Canadian' National
Railways	 56,527,000
Further estimates to be voted this year.. 7,500,000 Vote for branch terminals	 18,000,000
Total	$100,054,000
From this amount we subtract the apparent
surplus of $1,823,000, leaving a debt net or deficit of this country of $98,231,000. No one can deny any one of these figures, and I would like hon. gentlemen to note that I have omitted from this list the following
items:
Amount of refunding debt	$17,000,000
Amount to the Canadian Government
Merchant Marine	 900,000
To the Quebec Harbour Commissioners.. 600,000

And as we cannot obtain information as to whether these two amounts are for a certainty included in any other figures given by the minister, we will take it for granted and give the government the benefit of the doubt and leave them out. Therefore we come to this conclusion: that at the very least the additions of this year to the debt upon our country is $98,231,000. I know, Mr. Speaker, that other hon. members will find1 items in the budget that they will say should be added to it, but as an ordinary member I am taking figures that cannot be disputed. And, taking this minimum amount, can this government or any member of it say that we have a balanced budget? The statement has been made, and no doubt will be made in the future that the budget has been balanced; but in the face of this statement which I have submitted, and any manipulation of the figures by a minister of the crown or by an official of the crown to-prove a balanced budget, how can we describe such a statement except by saying that it is untrue and misleading? Some members may use stronger language and in doing so may incur the displeasure of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), who, in dealing with this budget has climbed up the back stairs of the band wagon and is attempting to iplay the big drum; but so far as we are concerned we will continue to make our affirmation in whatever language we like to use that the budget is not balanced. And in the last few years no Minister of Finance has claimed a balanced budget. Our public debt is mounting by leaps and1 bounds under this government having this year increased by the large sum of $98,231,000.
Now, sir, let us look at it from another angle-I am not making this statement as a chartered accountant but just as an ordinary member of the House. From time to time

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
statements are made that our debt has been reduced so many dollars. For a number of years this government has been dedaring at the end of each year that there has been a surplus. These statements are made with the intention of leading ordinary members of the House and the public to believe that the debt of the country is being gradually reduced. We can only take the statements year by year and ascertain whether during that period we have added any amount to the net public debt or not. An hon. member said the other day that he had been "flimflammed" by the budget. It is rather late at this time to learn this lesson, but it is better late than never. Yes, we and the country have been flimflammed by the statements of this government. I should like to call the attention of the House to two or three of those statements. It has been claimed by this government that taxes are decreasing. Just as I have shown in my statement about the sales tax, cheque tax and transportation tax, I want to show how the taxes have been "decreasing" upon the people of this country. Another claim made by the government is that they are practising a certain amount of economy. The position puts one in mind of whittlers round the country stores who are armed with a jack-knife and a stick, do nothing but whittle and accumulate about them a lot of shavings, with nothing manufactured, nothing achieved, nothing gained. The government has been whittling at economy for quite a number of years, and I should like to draw the attention of the House to certain results of the efforts of this combination of whittlers across the way. They whittled at the Civil Service, cutting out some little bumps, while they allowed others to grow larger. Under this operation the Auditor General's department increased by $17,000 a year by the addition of one employee. They whittled at the Department of National Defence, cutting out eight clerks, six stenographers and seven file clerks, but they added five clerk typists and three senior stenographers. They whittled out an inspector of harness and saddlery and added one inspector of leather products. They whittled out one inspector Of cloth and one inspector of clothing, and they added two inspectors of textile products. They whittled out one packer and one helper and they added two office appliance operators. They whittled out one messenger clerk and they added two office boys. They whittled down pensions by $60,000, but they increased the expense of the Pension board by $13,000. They whittled at the combines stick, and they have not reduced a single combine, although they have spent $50,000 in the whittling. They whittled at the Public Works expenditure, and while they were whittling the cost of the Scribe hotel mounted from $2,000,000 to $3,000,000. Tills has been the style of economy they have practised in spite of t'heir declaration as to what they were going to do according to their great plan marked out in 1919. I would like to read that. The statement begins:
Whereas, on the 31st March, last-
That is 1919-
-according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, the net public debt was $1,584,000,000, or, roughly, $220 for every man. woman and child in the Dominion, involving an annual interest charge of about $115,000,000; . . . .
And whereas, national disaster will overtake this country should the present method of financing the country's affairs be continued. . . .

Be it and it is hereby resolved that the serious nature of the country's financial situation calls for the profoundest consideration of all patriotic citizens, and the exercise of the severest economy by the government; that increase of revenue must be sought from an equitable and effective imposition and collection of graduated taxes, on business profits and income, applicable to all incomes above reasonable exemptions.
I have given the House an example of the "economy" practised by this government in regard to the income and business profits taxes showing that these have been constantly decreasing while the direct tax upon the ordinary people has been increasing.
I should like also to refer to the question of an export tax on power. I think it can be taken for granted that the people of Ontario, at least the part known as eastern Ontario, are strongly opposed to this idea, for the following reasons. We are now faced with the impossibility of increasing our amount of power. This sale of power to the Americans will certainly further increase the lack of power to us on this side of the line and will also set up competition for the price of power unless something is done by the government. For these reasons eastern Ontario is strongly opposed to this export tax. That part of the province is crying today for power; and, as I said in a forme." address, power means a great deal in the economic life of the people of this province: it means a lessening in the purchase of coal. We feel therefore that our source of power which is at our door, on the St. Lawrence, should be available to us. We cannot afford to wait for the result of this great scheme which is mentioned to-day in the press: I refer to the investigation into the canalization of the St. Lawrence. It would take a number of years to produce power under that scheme, and Ontario requires power to-day. Our supply will be at an end in 1926 and this export tax will certainly lessen the amount available to us.
There is another point indirectly connected with the budget to which I shall now refer, and that is the criticism which has been levelled at the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I would point out that all that has been said to the detriment of our merchant marine is practically tantamount to a criticism of the shipbuilding powers and capacity of this country; it is absolutely a criticism of the men and the corporations that have been engaged in the business of building ships in Canada. I do not think that either this government or any other government or its followers can afford to indulge in criticism of this kind. I have here a little book from which I obtain my facts in regard to the

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
marine situation, and I learn that in 1883 Canada held third place in tonnage amongst the nations of the world; her tonnage then was 1,311.000. In 1907 she had slipped back to seventh place with a tonnage of 657,000, a decrease of 654,000 tons. In 1907, Mr. A. G. Baillie published this little book to which I have referred, showing that there was then a tonnage of 1.069.000 of foreign vessels in Canada, not one under the British flag, employing 20,000 foreign seamen and thus debarring from work that number of Canadians. In 1916 Canada had gone back still further, occupying the sixteenth place. In 1915 there were 200.000.000 bushels of Canadian wheat for shipment but not one Canadian ship to carry that product:	Canada
was a grocery man without a delivery wagon, thousands of customers calling for his supplies. In 1917 Premier Lloyd George cut out transportation of everything except war materials and the necessities

of life, and millions of barrels of apples, besides lumber, pit props, and so forth, remained in Canada without any chance of being delivered, thus causing a great loss to the people of this country. Canada had farmed out her shipping to the foreigner and so lost millions of dollars. Sixty per cent of Canada's wheat crop in 1917 was shipped through foreign ports and the farmers paid in excess freight alone to foreign ships some $120,000,000. or $15,000,000 more than was spent in the building of the merchant marine. The situation in. British Columbia in 1915 was critical. Australia was calling for apples and potatoes but there were no ships available, while India was demanding railway ties, _ of which one cargo had been shipped on a foreign boat, other orders which had been given having to go by the board because there were no ships to carry them. Not one British Columbia built ship, it is said in this book, was in the foreign trade. And the situation on the Atlantic was about as bad in 1916. Captain Alexander ,T. Fraser, of Rexton, New Brunswick, found forty-two ships loading lumber on the Miramichi river, not one of them flying the British flag; they were all Scandinavian with the exception of two whioh were Russian. Thirty were wooden vessels which paid for themselves in one voyage. So that our merchant marine was built under very critical conditions; the ships were perhaps rather small inasmuch as the war had proven that the loss of large liners and steamers made serious inroads into the world's tonnage, so that it would be more economical to construct smaller vessels. These were the facts during the war, although of course the post-war conditions
were different. Now, these Canadian vessels, which have been subject to too much criticism, are not so poor in quality as the critics across the way try to make out. They were built by Canadians at a time when the demand for vessels of that size was greatest, and as this matter indirectly touches the budget I would point out to the House that the criticism which has been directed at our merchant marine is really a criticism of the shipbuilding industry of Canada, which we should encourage rather than injure in any way.
There are some other matters which I should like, to touch upon, such as, for instance: the defence of our Pacific coast; the culture of our fisheries; assistance to develop our ores in this country; the wastage of our natural resources; and the effect of the ooal tax. But I am going to leave these points for a future occasion. I want now to sum up certain features of the present situation in Canada; and before proceeding I will observe that it has been sufficiently established that the government in the present budget have demonstrated that instead of reducing they have increased the debt as well as the taxation of the country. I do not want the House to go away with the impression that the government have not accomplished something; there are certainly 'things which they have accomplished and which I shall enumerate without going too much into details. The government have brought down a "balanced budget" at the expense of a tremendous skyscraping public debt; they have established a harbour at Belle River without Ships; they have established an elevator at Prince Rupert without grain; they have established an immigration office in Paris without immigrants; and they have succeeded in deporting more good red-blooded Canadians than have left the country in any other era, with all its factors, in all our history. The result, of their efforts has been so great along these lines that even one of their celebrated commissions joined in the exodus until it was called home by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb); I mean the pulpwood commission. The government have succeeded, too, in providing jobs for the best political hacks that have stood by them in past years; and to give them credit, they have accomplished one of the best things in the Department of Agriculture, they have procured a balanced ration for the hen.
Now, Sir, in view of this list of accomplishments the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has now decided to throw down the gauntlet and call on the fray. He has sent his colour sergeant to hoist the colours,
2352	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
to raise the standard, and the hon. member for Chambly and Vereheres (M. Archambau'lt) has unfurled the flag. The fight is not to be on these matters of paramount interest to Canadians, but again it is to be waged upon the graves in Flanders and upon the sorrows and the mistakes of the Great war. In other words, the great federal fight is now to be waged on the Ross rifle. I should like to say, by way of answer to a question which I put to the hon. member, and which he did not answer, that the adoption of this rifle cannot be laid at the door of the Conservative government. It was developed following the disadvantages which the British and Canadian troops laboured under in South Africa, through their rifles being outdistanced by the celebrated Mauser rifle with its better sighting. As a private in that war I know whereof I speak. The Ross rifle was assembled in Quebec, and it was adopted in 1906 on the recommendation of the then Minister of Militia in the Liberal government, Sir Frederick Borden. To show how for a few years the improvement of that rifle was secured practically through the influence of Conservative members of this House, I may say that in 1906 and 1907 the Northwest Mounted Police were armed with it, one thousand rifles having been sent out to them. But in a very short time they discarded the Ross rifle and returned to the Winchester and the Lee-Enfield. The Ross rifle was adopted in 1906 by general order No. 104. Complaints were made during that year by the Conservative members of the House as to its defects, and as a result an investigation was held at which witnesses from all parts of Canada were examined. One of those witnesses was the deputy minister of the department, Colonel Fiset. His evidence was that he knew nothing about it. But as director general of the medical services he must have known that year after year from various camps complaints were made about that rifle.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I leave it to the
House to decide. There is a difference between a Small Arms committee and a committee of experts, for which the minister is absolutely and entirely responsible. Now, before this Small Arms committee was formed an investigation was held on the complaints that came from members of the Northwest Mounted Police and the militia. To show how this rifle was foisted upon the militia, it is significant that during that investigation men who were in change of the camps and districts attended and were prepared to give evidence as to the defects of the rifle, but in the committee room they found the Minister of Militia facing them, and they decided that if they were to hold their positions they had better keep their information in their pookets; which they did. But a sergeant of the Northwest Mounted Police was brave enough to bear the brunt. In spite of a lot of brow-beating he stuck to his opinion as to the defects of the rifle. Thereupon the investigation was called off, with the intimation that it would be renewed in the Public Accounts committee the next year, but nothing more was ever heard of it. Then came the formation of the Small Arms committee, and the rifle having been improved in the meantime, in 1909 our men were able to take first

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
place at Bisley. From that time on no further complaints were heard until the change of government came, when it was found that a contract had been entered into by the former Minister of Militia with the Ross Rifle Company for delivery of many thousands of these rifles. Eighteen thousand were delivered in 1908, another thirty-eight thousand in 1909, and they were being delivered a thousand at a time right up to the outbreak of the Great war. Now, I think it was a great mistake for the hon. member for Chambly and Yer-cheres (Mr. Archaimbault) to blame the loss of our men at the front upon the defects of the Ross rifle. The adoption of the Ross rifle was an effort on Canada's part to develop a national small arms weapon, an attempt to have a rifle possessing long range and splendid sighting. But when the Great war came that rifle was found to be of no use in the trenches. It was too long, it was a straight-tpull rifle, and it had not undergone sufficient tests to prove whether or not it would jam. Unfortunately under actual war conditions it did jam, and no doubt lives were lost. But undoubtedly the earlier defects of the rifle had been pointed out by the Conservatives, and its improvement was due to the Conservatives, and if it had not been for their action our first division would likely have gone to France armed with the old Mark 1-and God knows what the disaster would have been in that event.
So that, if disasters followed the use of the Ross rifle, the improvement of it was the result of the continued complaints and demands for investigation. Even in 1908 there was a demand in the House of Commons for an investigation, which was refused by the then minister. It is too bad that these things have to be brought up. I am not speaking harshly of anybody; I know that accidents occurred and mistakes were made in the war. During that first fight of St. Julien the men were not experienced not only with the rifle but with other equipment they took very l'ttle care. On the plains of Salisbury we had to fit them out three times at the very least. We repeatedly drew their attention to the necessity of going out and keeping their water bottles full. All these things were forgotten by the men until the disaster came upon them, but from that day on there was an improvement in this respect, and the men benefited by their experience. If any party is to be blamed for the Ross rifle you might just as well blame them for the want of preparation in combating the gas, for which we were never prepared.
The second great point in this campaign over which the flag has been unfurled, in the fight that is to be waged, is that 100,000 unfit men reached England. I do not care to discuss that. As the late Deputy Minister of the Department of National Defence (Sir Eugene Fiset) knows well, it was all due to a want of proper medical examination. But in spite of 'hat I would point out that unfit men reached France and gave sufficient service there as unfit men to offset the S150,000,000 which was lost by the unfit men in England. I would say this, in answer to it all: If this is to be the slogan of the fight, then it is to be remembered that these men at least reached England, and that some of them reached France.
To pass on .quickly, I want to say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and this government have had a great heritage passed into their hands in the way of the mines, the forests and the other natural resources of this country. So far their policy has been one of dissipation, both in men and in natural resources. The natural resources are flowing in streams from the shores and the borders of this country. Our sons and daughters are passing in great numbers over our boundaries, and your graphs and figures and budgets are not preventing their exodus. Within the borders of our country the condition of our people is largely unheeded by this government. The present condition in one section particularly is a blot on our national life. Appeals have been made to this House, in the House and out of it, but they have not stirred the Prime Minister. Let me read to you his pledge and that of his party in this respect and ask whether this, another of the great pledges, is being fulfilled:
Therefore this gathering of Liberals in convention assembled pledges itself to a vigorous prosecution of the measures Ibest calculated to conserve the life and improve the physical standard of our Canadian
citizenship.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the appeals being made to this House and of the condition of the people in one section of the country- I refer to Cape Breton-I ask, is that pledge being fulfilled? Is the attention being given to the conserving of the life of our people in that part of the country which is pledged by the government in this undertaking? The excuse has been put up that this is a provincial matter. It is not so much a provincial matter; in a former address I pointed out that health was a Dominion matter and that federal relief had not been confined to largo or small cases; that it had been varied in its
2354	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
application. During the history of this country we have provided large amounts by way of relief for different purposes. In 1880 this country sent over to the relief of distressed Ireland, $100,000. In 1899 this parliament sent to the West India sufferers, $25,000. In 1902 this parliament sent to relieve the sufferers in connection with the volcanic disaster in the West Indies, $50,000. In 1900 the San Francisco earthquake and fire disaster was the occasion of a gift of $100,000 from this country. In 1907 and 1908 the sufferers through the earthquake in Jamaica received $50,000 from Canada. In 1909, $100,000 was contributed to the relief of sufferers from an earthquake in Italy. In 1915 the sum of $25,000 was granted by parliament in connection with the Newfoundland sealing disasters. In 1921 typhoid conditions in Europe were relieved by this parliament through a contribution of $200,000. Following the disaster at Halifax the Conservative government, or Union government, whatever you like to call it, brought down a vote of $25,000,000 for the sufferers there. In 1918 those affected by the disasters at New Waterford and Stellarton were assisted by the Union government .to the extent of $25,000, $10,000 going .to. New Waterford and $15,000 to Stellarton. Yet in the face of this condition the present appeal for relief falls upon stony hearts so far as this House is concerned, and we see our people suffer.
I am not going to say whether this condition is due to one cause or to another, but from the reports brought here and the appeals made it is evident that children 4 p.m. are suffering, that they are ill fed and poorly clad, and the result must be to bring about neurasthenic and tubercular conditions. The plight of the women is also a serious one. Looking at the children they have brought into the world and seeing them suffer for want of food must produce among them a neurotic or neurasthenic condition from which they may suffer for years to come. Amongst the men, if this strike condition continues, there will develop a spirit of spite, hatred and malice, followed, perhaps, by murder and arson. All these things are a blot upon our national life and should not be allowed to continue. Grant that it is an industrial conflict; then, Sir, I would point out that we have at the head of this government a man who is by experience most capable of dealing with just such a situation, according to his own words. I have here a pamphlet published by himself containing a speech which he delivered in parliament outlin-

ing his services in connection with the adjustment of relations between workers and employers in war industries. Now, Sir, a man who has had that experience should be best able to cope with a comparatively small matter of adjustment such as that which now demands attention in Cape Breton. In this pamphlet he is given the credit of solving the problems connected with the industrial civil war then taking place in the industries of the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company. He was thanked by the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company for his services on that occasion. He settled the difficulties in connection with the Bethlehem Steel Company plant, according to this statement, and he adjusted the differences between the Standard Oil Company and its workers in Indiana, when the men received an increase of 11.11 per cent in wages and a six-day . week. Here, Sir, is a little David who went, out against these industrial giants of another country and settled all1 these problems. Yet a festering sore exists in our own Dominion and nobody has the courage to come and settle it.
I might refer to other conditions. The exodus is an old story in this House. The existence of the exodus is denied yet it is still going on. I read to-day in the paper that twenty-five men a day are leaving Cape Breton, and I have here another item which speaks of greater numbers leaving. I do not know the man who is at the head of the latter movement but I want to say that many of the men in Cape Breton are war veterans and they have my sympathy. The clipping that I have refers to a Glace Bay war veteran, A. R. MacDonald, who up to 1914, when he returned home to join the Canadian Expeditionary force, spent several years in the Argentine. He is one of the movers of this scheme, open to returned men only, under which it is proposed to take a colony of about one thousand men from Cape Breton to the Argentine. Mr. MacDonald is quoted as saying:	"Under the government we now have
in Canada, the chanices are that this number" 

he is speaking of the 100,000 ex-service men who have been expatriated to the United States-"will be augmented considerably this year." He adds that if suitable arrangements can be made with the Argentine government a thousand veterans will be moved from the Glace Bay district. I have also received this morning another communication which contradicts the claim that conditions are satisfactory in Canada. There was an election in West Hastings. I am waiting for the cheers from hon. gentlemen opposite.

This is a letter which was sent out this morning, I think other members of the House received a copy:
Dominion Combing Mills Limited, Trenton Dear Sir.-
1.	Are you aware of the fact that the action of the Department of Customs in not enforcing the Customs Act is equivalent to discrimination against our firm ?
2.	Items 555 and 556 of customs tariff are not being enforced.
3.	The Commissioner of Customs and his staff are aware of this and admit the facts.
4.	This duty was placed on the statute to encourage someone to establish a key industry.
5.	After investigating the matter and being assured there was a duty on wool tops, we established the finest combing mill in the world at Trenton, Ontario, capable of taking care of the entire requirements of all the worsted spinners in Canada.
6.	Over 15,000 citizens of Canada are financially interested in the success of this company and all the wool growers in Canada, and numerous other industries, will profit by its success.
7.	The failure of the government to enforce and collect the duty as called for, means a loss of over half a million dollars a year in revenue, on wool and wool tops, and a severe hardship to the shareholders in thi3 company.
8.	The officials of the department claim that they cannot enforce this duty without instructions from the Finance Minister.
9.	As one of the law makers of this country, will you please call the attention of the Finance Minister to the unfairness to us in this matter, and use your best influence to have the law properly administered.
I predict that as a result of this situation this large industry, one of the finest that we have in Canada will soon pass into history like many other of our woollen mills.
In conclusion I wish to say that the present budget, like the former three which have been brought' down under the present administration, demonstrates that this government has failed in its promises of economy, reduction of the public debt, and reduction of government costs. It has failed in its efforts to lower the cost of living, to break combines, to give employment to the people. In the discussion on the unemployment situation which has taken place the government have admitted that our only hope is in the provinces; that their own hands are tied and that they are as helpless as a new 'bom babe; that the words of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour are as sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal. It is apparent that the Prime Minister and his sleeping partners can no longer inspire enthusiasm and hope in the hearts of the people, many of whom have migrated to fields of greater hopes whilst many more are still going. This condition will continue until the country awakens to new life under a new policy and a new
leader-a new leader who will introduce a policy which shall protect, and in protecting upbuild again and develop the shattered industries of Canada, including our great primary industry of agriculture.

speechtext:
No, my contribution to the cost will not amount to very many dollars, but I can assure my hon. friend that if he objects I will be willing to turn the amount back into the treasury.
The tariff is brought up every year and discussed ad infinitum. I have been in this House for over eight years. I have listened to the various discussions upon the tariff, and so far they have left me cold. I do not believe that any one member in this House during the past fifty years has changed his vote as the result of the debate on this question of the tariff. If he changed his vote it was for some reason other than the tariff; the tariff was given as the reason for it. The tariff has been attacked on the one side for its inadequacy and on the other for its iniquity. But we have the tariff with us, and we shall always have it. It is impossible for this country to get on without a tariff. I think every hon. gentleman will admit that. If we have a tariff it should be in my humble opinion one that will protect us against other countries. What is the use of a tariff that will not protect? We may as well have no tariff at all. It is only natural that I should express views of this kind, coming from the district from which I come. It is possible that if I lived in a western province I would hold vastly different views from those which I hold now. It is a matter of atmosphere, geography and votes. Votes, after all, are the most important thing. So that when I hear people talking patriotically about the tariff it makes me smile. It is purely, as I said before, a question of geography and nothing else. After all, what does tariff tinkering amount to at the present time? We have got beyond the point of appealing on the question of the tariff. Suppose we raised the tariff on this item or on that item two and a half per cent, or lowered it two and a half per cent, do hon. members think that will affect the country? I say that it will not. We have reached the condition of affairs now that the financial condition of the country and the success of our country are not going to depend upon the question of the tariff, but on other and more important questions. The railway question, for instance, is the most important matter in the country. We had some figures from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marier)-and I am sure no person will controvert those figures-to show that this country has paid out to the National Railways in one form or another within the last five years between five and six hundred millions of dollars. How long are we going to be able to continue? If we are going to per-
mit this condition to continue it spells ruin for the country. There is only one solution of this whole question, and that is, instead of having two lines in this country, one-half nationalized and one-half privately owned, we should have one line owned by one or the other, either the government or the privately-owned company. Now the privately-owned company is the Canadian Pacific. I think every hon. gentleman here will admit that the Canadian Pacific has made a success of the running of its lines. It is the most successful and the best managed railway company in the world. And in competition with that we have the Dominion of Canada also running a railway line. The duty of the government of Canada is to govern the country. The duty of a railway company is to run the railway. Now will any person suggest that the Dominion of Canada can run a railway company better than the Canadian Pacific?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know what he said about that, but I do not think any person can object to the service on the Canadian National. It is first-class in every respect. There is nothing better in the world than the service on the Canadian National? And why? Because the Dominion of Canada is at the back of it to pay the piper, without any regard at all for economy. When they need money they say, "Send seven million" or "Give us ten million," or "Give us fifteen million." and like Moses when he struck the rock, the water gushes forth.

speechtext:
I should like to interject the' remark that last week a gentleman who had just returned from Australia was in my office,

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs
and stated that the service given there was very good, and that shower baths were provided on the trains in Australia.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Very good. That shows
they have a little water in their stock. For the last two or three days the newspapers have been filled with a surprising bit of information, a discovery made by Sir Henry Thornton, that if the two 'lines were amalgamated, the combined lines would pay the fixed charges of these two railways. That is quite an important piece of information. It is the first bit of good news we have received from the Canadian National's head for some time. That information was given us in 1921 by Lord Shaughnessy. He told us exactly the. same thing as Sir Henry Thornton told us a day or two ago. The Shaughnessy plan, hon. members will remember, was a scheme whereby the Canadian Pacific would take over the Canadian National Railways, eliminate duplication and overlapping, co-ordinate the two lines, and have them run as one; and he proposed that, in consideration of that, their fixed charges would be assumed and a dividend in perpetuity would be paid to the stockholders of the Canadian Pacific. That did not seem to be an unreasonable thing. If they turn over their line they want something in return for it, and that seems only reasonable. What are the figures? As I calculate them, about $35,000,000 per annum is the amount which this government would be asked to guarantee. Now in consideration of that sum, they would take over the Canadian National lines. Lord Shaughnessy in effect proposed that if by some arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway certain assets, not being strictly railway property, could be segregated, and the railway property added to the government system, the system would comprise 31,000 miles of railway with a considerable number of parallel lines unimportant or useless. The consideration to be given the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in exchange for the properties above defined would be in the nature of an undertaking by the government of Canada to pay to the shareholders in perpetuity, a fixed annual dividend on the Share capital, to be supplemented by a further payment when the whole property was yielding a specified return. The extraneous assets of the Canadian Pacific Railway would be transferred to and be administered by trustees or by a subsidiary company with another board of directors, so that the directors of the railway company would be interested only in the administration of the trust placed in their hands by the people of Canada. There would be no motive
for selfishness, if such a thing were possible in the circumstances. The income on their shares being fixed and unchangeable, excepting as above provided, the Canadian Pacific Railway shareholders could receive no advantage from preferential treatment given to any particular portion of the railway system. The directorate would have every incentive for wise, prudent and business-like administration.
These were the broad principles of the plan. As to details, the political management was ruled out as impossible and ruinous and the proposal made that the existing Canadian Pacific Railway management be utilized under the terms of a contract approaching perpetuity in its duration, to administer and operate the whole property for account of the Canadian people. Under the consolidation, and taking 1920 figures as a basis, the gross earnings would be $342,283,000 and the operating expenses $345,973,000; to the latter would have to be added the annual fixed charges of the whole system, the guaranteed dividend on Canadian Pacific Railway preference and common stock, and incidentals; the resulting total deficit would be about $SO,000,000. Against this Lord Shaughnessy added a possible saving of $56,000,000 bv bringing the combined average of operating costs to the Canadian Pacific level, a saving of about $12,000,000 by reducing these costs four per cent or five per cent more, in years less expensive than 1920 which he thought possible, with the balance easily wiped out by improved conditions of national settlement and development.

Of course, Sir Henry
Thornton so far has been a splendid promiser. speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
just stated what I had in mind, that no discussion is permissible of proceedings before a committee which has not yet reported to the House. I supposed the hon. gentleman referred1 to what appeared in the papers of yesterday, and that is quite a different matter.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was particular to do that,
but the chairman of the committee (Mr. Euler) probably thought he was a law unto himself and could transgress the rules. What I said was this, that anything that the Canadian National Railways under government ownership can do for us, the Canadian Pacific can certainly do. They have been in the business for forty years. Their business is to run rail-[DOT] ways. They have made a success of their railways. In our case, as I have already intimated, we cannot run railways because we are too busy governing the country. That is our business, and I doubt whether we have succeeded in it. This Dominion cannot be a maid-of-all-work. We must restrict our

energies to what we are sent here to do and nothing else. I do not know whether hon. members realize the feeling of uneasiness throughout the whole of Canada with regard to this railway situation. We feel that our money is being thrown into a bottomless pit; that every dollar we put into this railway we shall never get back; that we are simply preparing these railways, fitting them up, bringing them up to the mark in the hope that some day we shall be able to turn them over to some individual or company who can run them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We shall never be able to
get a cent of our money back. I do not agree with the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). I rather agree with the hon. member for Laprairie and Napier-ville (Mr. Lanctot) who said last year that he would sell the railways for a dollar -and has now reduced the sum to fifty cents -to anybody who would take them over and not ask us for another cent.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest a combination of the two lines and a government subsidy with control of rates?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My suggestion is that the
lines should be amalgamated in order that we might never hear the word "subsidy" again; that we should close the door on it, lock the door and throw away the key. I wonder whether hon. gentlemen realize that about 34 cents of every dollar which we collect by any form of taxation from the people of this country goes to the upkeep of the Canadian National railways. Do hon. gentlemen realize that the $50,000,000 which we collect from the income tax pays about 40 per cent ol our loss on the Canadian National Railways? How long is it possible for us to go on and pay in that way? There must be a limit tc it at some time. There seems to be nothing at the present moment except promises that at some time in the dim and misty future we shall be blessed by having a line which will not cost us anything further in the way of outlay to run. But I am not the optimist that the hon. member for North Waterloo is. I believe that as long as we have this line, it will be a white elephant on our hands; that it is going to bleed us white, and that if we do not take care as to the future, the time may come when there will be a question of repudiation of the debt on this line as well as the debt of Canada to others.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have been trying to find out, listening to this debate, what are

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs
the total liabilities of the Canadian National Railways on which we are paying interest. Can the hon. member tell us what they are?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no idea. I am afraid to look up to find out. I am frightened to know what the figure is. The hon. gentleman as well as others perhaps ought to be satisfied to know that it is a very large sum and not to know the real facts.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How would the hon. member
view the proposal to amalgamate the two lines and put the Canadian Pacific organization in charge just as the Canadian National organization under Sir Henry Thornton is in charge now? Would he expect that they would get out of debt and put the railway on a good foundation?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What I am trying to argue is that when we eliminate competition, we shall be in a much better position than we are now. We have duplication, overlapping, want of co-operation. Sir Henry Thornton said the other day: "I spent $1,100,000 last year and I intend to continue advertising because I think it is a good thing for my company to do." If we had one line of railway, there would be no necessity for advertising. People would have to take that line or walk. That is only one instance. We would be cutting out all these lines running in a parallel direction from one city to another. I have in mind Ottawa where we have nine railway trains every day taking down a handful of people to Montreal. It is criminal to do a thing of that kind, and all through this country you find the same condition prevailing. It is absurd that we should have our line in competition with another line, and the result is that neither of them can be made to pay. The Canadian Pacific last year barely met their dividend charges. I think they had about $100,000 over, and a large portion of that was taken from proceeds which were earned not out of the line proper.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member argue
that the Canadian Pacific organization is much more efficient than the Canadian National organization?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not prepared to say
that they are more efficient, but I am prepared to say that we want only one efficient road rather than two inefficient roads. This country has a population of eight or nine million people, becoming less every day, as I shall be able to show before I conclude. We have not room in this country for practically three transcontinental lines. The
United States, with their population of 115,000,000 have not one transcontinental line; there is not one uninterrupted line from coast to coast in that country. In Canada on the other hand we had at one time three transcontinental railways. Now, we have room for one, and my proposition is that one of these lines, the Canadian Pacific, should take over the other lines in Canada under some such plan as has been outlined by Lord Shaughnessy. I do not say that we should at once fall in with that scheme, but it is a basis for negotiations. We might be able to work out something, however, if we adopted that plan, that might be better for the people of the country and for the Canadian Pacific Railway as well.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that there is now, or ought to be at least, less wasteful competition and overlapping than when, instead of the Canadian National Railways, we had three competing systems?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We had three competing
systems apart from the Canadian Pacific
and there was a lot of waste. But how did that waste occur? No one knows better than my right hon. friend.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We had Mackenzie and
Mann every year in the lobbies, and they got away with $25,000,000 on one occasion and $45,000,000 on another; many millions of dollars did they draw from the coffers of this country in order to run these wasteful lines. That is what happened; but thank God that is all a matter of the past; let us hope that we shall have no more of that. Sir William Mackenzie has gone to his reward and the haunts of Sir Donald Mann know him no more. I think that perhaps the people of this country have learned a great many things since the war, and they have learned many things since taking over these lines. They have found that these lines were not run for the profit of the country nor for the profit of the stockholders of Mackenzie and Mann, but for the profit of half a dozen buccaneers who made away with all this money and left us holding the bag.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then the hon. gentleman agrees that the amalgamation of the three systems was a good thing?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, the amalgamation of the three would be a good thing.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: " Was " a good thing.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was no amalgamation of the three.
The Budget (Mr. Jacobs)

Mr.	MEIGHEN: Yes,-the	Canadian
Northern, the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am willing to admit that that was the only alternative we had; we could only amalgamate them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think the right hon. gentleman had any option; with him it was a case of Hobson's choice.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What about a
traffic arrangement with the Canadian National and the Grand Trunk at the time of the question of the purchase of the Grand Trunk?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I don't get that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I mean, what
about a traffic arrangement as another alternative?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I am talking about the time the question was discussed of acquiring the Grand Trunk railway. What does the hon. gentleman think, as another alternative at that time, of a traffic arrangement between the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National Railways? That alternative was proposed in this House.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think it would have come to anything, because eventually these lines would have had to be taken over and be amalgamated, as they were. I may say frankly that at the time it was done I was rather violently opposed to it, but I have come to believe that there was nothing else for the country to do than to take them over. And now there is nothing else to be done than to give these lines over to the Canadian Pacific.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give them?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Turn them over under the Shaughnessy plan: or some similar arrangement.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has made a strong criticism of the " buccaneers " of the railway world in years gone by. Is that not a criticism of private ownership, under which these things occurred?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend does not suggest that every private person is a buccaneer.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say anything about buccaneers; it was the hon. member himself who used that term.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am referring to certain gentlemen in particular whose names I have no wish to mention, although they are not in this House, 'who got away with all this money and left the lines on our hands.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Under private ownership.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Private ownership is one thing and buccaneer ownership another. Now, as I said before, we have a population of eight or nine millions to support these two lines, and it will be admitted by everyone, I think, that we do not want two lines in this country. There are gentlemen in this House, in fact I think the same is true of all hon. members, who want only one line; there is not a person who wants two. The question however is, who will run them? Should it be the Canadian government or the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? In this connection I am reminded of one of the Bab Ballads, about the cook and the mate of a ship who were both stranded on an island and who after a time found it necessary to resort to cannibalism. The mate said something like this, "You ought to let me eat you, seeing that I am more in authority than yourself." But the cook did not see it in that light; he said, '"I would be glad to accommodate you, but I am a cook and can prepare meals much better than you can. Why should you want to cook me when you are not a cook?" That is the position to-day in regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National system; the Canadian Pacific knows how to run railways; they are the cooks, whereas the others are merely mates and nothing else.
As to the suggestion that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be taken over by the Canadian National Railways, I do not think that those who make a proposal of this kind have thought of what the additional cost would be, and that is something that appals me. I am sure there is not a public man in this country who would think of taking over the Canadian Pacific Railway, with everything that that implies, and incorporating it with, I was going to say, a corpse, -at any rate, with something that would be a corpse if we withdrew from it the support which we give it from day to day.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why not put the excellent
Canadian Pacific Railway organization in charge of the combined railways? Why

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.
should not the country amalgamate the two systems, taking over the Canadian Pacific with its excellent organization, and, if that organization is much better than that of the Canadian National, giving it control?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would object to that because the ultimate power would be in the hands of my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good), of my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brcwn), of myself and other members of parliament. And we do not want railways. That is my reason for wanting the Canadian National turned over to a company which would be under no obligations to the government and would not look to the government for support. You give a man a crutch or a stick and he will lean upon it for support until after a while he will not be able to walk straight. We want all the lines brought under an efficient management such as we find in the Canadian Pacific Railway, the best managed railway in the world. I am sure we could make a success of the combination. What has been shown is that under an amalgamation of the two lines there would be no loss. The deficit of the Canadian National Railway system last year was $57,000,000 and the addition to the funded and unfunded debt was $119,000,000. Can we sit quietly by and allow this sort of thing to go on, when we are told by the heads of the railways that all that is necessary to eliminate loss is an amalgamation of the two systems? That is a question I put to hon. gentlemen.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was not the proposed guarantee of the minimum of ten per cent, which the Canadian Pacific wanted, a crutch?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. Three per cent of that ten per cent comes from the land department of the Canadian Pacific Railway; and then there is the ocean service, which would not go in. What they want is a guarantee of the dividends which they have been able to pay their stockholders for the last twenty-five years. And that is reasonable. They are earning the dividends now and have been earning them for years. Why should they make any arrangement that would endanger these dividends to their stockholders, giving them nothing in return? They want to have those dividends turned into bonds and to have a guarantee of $35,000,000 a year, a paltry sum having regard to the very vast amounts which we have been paying out since taking over the Canadian National Railways. And they say that when this is done the lines will be amalgamated and they will be able to show by figures that there will be no loss to the 151
country, while the fixed charges will be met from year to year.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All this is very interesting
and we are getting information, but I want to ask the hon. gentleman a question. If all the railways in the country were run by a private corporation, would he still be in favour of having the railway commission fix the rates? Otherwise, would not the country be entirely at the mercy of the company?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The line would be controlled by the railway commission, who would fix rates, indicate what branch lines were to be built, and so on, as they do at the present time. The railway company would be the creature of the railway commission. There is no suggestion at all that the railway commission should be abolished. Such a suggestion would not work. I grant you that if this vast monopoly were to begin to function without some regulative body such as the railway commission, it would be a disastrous thing for the country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If that be so, what happens to government interference that my hon, friend was criticizing?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is not government interference.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All the railway commission's decisions are subject to revision by the government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
After all, public opinion
counts for something.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does here also.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There may have been some little sporadic criticism of the railway commission from my friends on the opposite side, but it was well-intentioned criticism, and I do not think they ever questioned the honesty or integrity of the commission.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman
looked up the recent life history of the Minister of Agriculture?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am afraid my right hon.
friend was taking the Minister of Agriculture seriously on that occasion. I think it may be gathered from the remarks I have made this afternoon that I am not quite in favour of public ownership of railways. I wish to make that clear to the House. I have always been opposed to public ownership when private ownership can be made to apply, because I believe in the efficiency of private ownership. I believe that private ownership has been able to accomplish almost everything that has been accomplished so far in this wcrld, and that

23G2
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.

public ownership, or the interference by governments and by governing bodies generally, has always been a brake and detriment to progress. I am talking generally. In any event I throw out these suggestions for what they are worth. I feel that the temper of the people is in favour of some change in our railway policy, and that the sooner we do something along these lines the better it will be for the government and for the country. Our people will not stand very much more of this tinkering with our railway system. It is a running sore, it is something which must be cured. We have to do something, and at once; and my suggestion, I hope, is a fair solution of the problem. I have yet to hear from any public man in Canada that the taking over of the Canadian Pacific line by the Canadian National, running as it is, is going to meet with the approval of this country. To me it is just like taking a healthy child who has never been sick and putting him to bed with a sick child suffering from a contagious disease. That is exactly parallel to what would be done if we put the Canadian Pacific Railway in with the Canadian National Railways.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you think you would have had those advances from the Canadian Pacific Railway a few years ago. before the Canadian National Railways made the showing they have made under the present management?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you mean advances looking to an arrangement?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is when they did come.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They were not suffering at that time, because they were making hay while the sun was shining-they were dealing with cripples at that time. But to-day it has become a very serious matter for the Canadian Pacific Railway. They feel they are pitted against the government of Canada, and it is a fight to the death. Everyone knows what the result will be.
Now, as I said before, we have a population of less than 9,000,000, and there is a general complaint throughout the country that we are losing our people at an alarming rate. It is true. Last year, according to the returns of the United States Bureau-our own government does not keep any returns,-we lost to that country 159,000 of our population; that is people who paid their head tax and went through in the ordinary way. They were credited to Canada,-if I may so term it. What
[Mr. Jacobs.!
kind of people go from this country to the United States now under the quota law? Our native-born; only those are taken in. What becomes of the foreign-bom in Canada? They go in by the underground route.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not go.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They all stay here?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Out -west, anyway, they stay.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am surprised to hear that. I thought they migrated to the United States in about equal proportions. The.fact that a man is foreign-born does not make very much difference if he wants to go to the United States. At any rate, we will say a certain number of them went. Perhaps they are so satisfied in the region of Brandon that they do not leave for the United States. That is not the experience down my way. I know the United States immigration office is besieged from morning to night by people who are trying to obtain the necessary permission to enter that country. At a rough computation I would say about a hundred thousand of those people went to 'the United States. How many immigrants did we bring into Canada last year? We brought 140.000. What kind of people came in? Half British bom and half foreign bom. Now, as I said before, the vast majority of the people who went to the United States are Canadian-born -a much better class, I grant you, than the foreign-born. Why is it that these people have gone in such numbers to the United States? I know my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition will say that it is because of the lack of tariff in this country. I do not know how far that is true, but I think my right hon. friend is magnifying the number of people who went to the United States because of poor tariff conditions here. Our people who crossed the line did so because there is no quota law preventing their entry into the United States. Are hon. members aware that the government of the United States 'has put into effect a quota law which prevents more than 2 per cent of any nationality entering that country, based on the number of that nationality who came there before 1890?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I may be wrong, hut does
not that quota law prevent not only foreign-bom but British-born going to the United States?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It prevents English-born
no more than foreign-bom; 2 per cent of any nationality* are allowed entrance. It makes no difference if the immigrants are

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.
descended from the angel Gabriel; they cannot enter the United States if more than 2 per cent of them 'have already come in during that year. What happens? We have the United States declaring by law that the only people who can enter their country in unlimited numbers as against the rest of the world are the Canadian-born. What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that Canada is being drained of her native-born to satisfy the demands of the United States. It is only a question of a very short time, unless diplomatic representations are made to the United States, before every native-born Canadian will be walking the streets of Chicago, Detroit, Boston or other American city, and we may see a specimen in our museum stuffed and properly mounted to show what a native-born Canadian was once like.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me? Irrespective of any quota law restrictions, what is his explanation of why our Canadian-born should want to go to the United States?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it is thei law of
gravitation, I suppose; the greater attracts the lesser.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They did not a while
ago.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There never was such an
exodus to the United States as there has been since the quota law was put into operation. So you have cause and effect side by side. Never befdre did they have such a law in the United States, and never before did we have so many Canadians migrating to that country. So it seems to me clear that this policy on the part of the United States is designed to drain this country of the best element that we have, and1 after a while Canada will be as bare of our native-born as Jacques Cartier found her in 1534.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would not my hon. friend admit that if the larger proportion of those who are going to the United States could get work in Canada they would remain here?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They may and they may
not. The spirit of adventure is strong in the young Anglo-Saxon. ,He likes to go abroad, to seek for adventure. He wants to know what the world is like before he settles down. And then distant hills look green: he thinks Detroit is a (paradise, that Chicago is the door leading to paradise, and so on. Everything looks well to him until he arrives, 151*
and then he finds that things are not quite as he would like them to be, but he has cut the painter and he cannot go back. The point I am trying to make is this: This policy on the part of the United States is designed for the purpose of drawing from this country the best element we have. Why not allow naturalized foreign-born Canadians to go into the United States? Surely in every respect they are as good as the others. Suppose a man happens to have been bom in Germany, or born in England, or bom, if you will, in Scotland-and I think the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) will admit that you cannot get a higher type than the Scotch; and I am almost inclined to agree with him, that Scotchman or that German or that Englishman, under the present regulation, will have to be put on the quota provided for by the United States with regard to the country from which he came; he cannot go in as a native-born Canadian. Of course that keeps out all the other foreign-born Canadians, and as I have suggested, it is only a question of time when we will have only foreign-born in this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask a question? If
Canada were to put on a quota law to reduce the number of foreign immigrants coming into this country, might not some of those native-born Canadians be inclined then to stay at home?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend like
to make the experiment?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not object at all.
I would be very much in favour of it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will
agree that these experiments in the matter of immigration are dangerous. They are not practical; they are not natural; they come to nothing. If you want immigration into this country, open the doors and let the people come in, but do not say, we do not want this man because his hair is red, or we do. not want this man because his teeth are long-let them come in and let them work out their own destiny in this country. To pursue a different policy is a mistake, in my opinion. In the United States they have this quota law 'because, they say, " We have already too many people in our country. We have 115,000,000 and we do not want any more. We want to digest those we have; we want to make men out of them; we want to give them an opportunity to acquaint themselves with and adopt American ideals before we bring in any more."
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If that is the case, why does not the United States apply the quota law against us?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because they want our few Canadian born citzens in their country-they want them. I suppose one of the reasons may be that we have such a large frontier, consisting of practically 4,000 miles, and it is almost impossible to keep them out-but that would apply to the foreign born as well. I am not in the secrets of the statesmen of the United States, but the fact remains that they will permit Canadian bom citizens to go into their country without let or hindrance and with regard tc others they are permitting only 2 per cent to go in. These are the bald facts.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? If it is the attraction really of large population or the lure of distance that draws our people to the United States, why is it that they do not go to England?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Our people?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a farfetched argument.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I do not know why they do not go to England. Perhaps the fact that they would have to walk 3,000 miles across the Atlantic might have something to do with it-that may be one of the reasons. Perhaps we could send them on the right hon. gentleman's merchant marine or the Petersen ships.
Now what I desired to point out was that this law was designed to withdraw from this country the best element of our population. The United States are making a distinction Between different types of British citizens in Canada. They pay no attention to the fact that a man who is a British citizen has his naturalization certificate. They say that is of no account with them; they treat that certificate as a scrap of paper. I would like to draw to the attention of the House something that happened in the United States in 1912. There was a treaty between the United States and Russia up to that time passed ia 1832, under which the United States traded freely with Russia, and generally the two countries were on terms of international intimacy. A short time prior to 1912 the Russian government enacted a law which provided that people of Jewish persuasion, although holders of American naturalization certificates, would cot be permitted to enter Russia. There was one exception-they allowed bankers to come

in. Unless they were bankers they could not come in. President Taft took the
5. p.m. matter up diplomatically at the time with the Russian government, pointing out that American citizens must all be treated alike, regardless of race or creed. The Russian government at that time pnd up to the revolution were the most reactionary in the world, and they refused to accept the views of President Taft. Accordingly the treaty was denounced, the President of the United States refusing to agree to any proposal under which a distinction would be made between different classes of American citizens. But now, in the year of grace, 1925, another rules in his place, and we have discrimination made -with regard to Canada in the matter of race, in the matter of nationality, by the declaration that if you are not a Canadian-born citizen, whether you have a British naturalization certificate or not, you cannot go into that country. Well, I say that is a matter which ought to be treated diplomatically between this country and the United States. We ought to deal with the United States in the same way that they deal with us. We ought to make them recognize that they have duties as a great state to perform towards other states. We cannot very well object to their allowing our native born to go into their country, but we ought to say: If you are taking them in, you must take them all in or none.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would that not increase the number of Canadians going to the United States?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would-that is rather
obvious. But the point of my argument is that if you increase the number going to the United States you probably would get fewer Canadian born to go, and they might be prepared over there to accept the number two article, that is, the foreign born. The result might be to leave a few of the Canadian born in this country; because I should hesitate to think that if I wanted to see a real Canadian I would have to go outside of Canada to see him.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Could he tell the House when the United States adopted this quota law?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There were two laws adopted. One was adopted some time during the war, fixing the quota at 3 per cent and the year as 1910. After that it was found not to work effectively enough. In July, 1924, it was reduced to 2 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
