speechtext: The first was not applicable to Canada at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, the first was not applicable to Canada at all.
Now, how have we dealt with the question of bringing people into the country in order to make good the loss which is constantly taking place by this migration? I am not a medical 'man and if I am wrong in my theory there are some hon. members who will check me up, but when patients suffer from hemorrhages the doctor prescribes some blood-producing food in order to make good the loss induced by the hemorrhage. I think my hon. friend from Port William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) remembers enough medicine to say whether that is true or not.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is almost
as good a doctor as he is a lawyer.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for
the compliment. Now, how do we deal with the situation? We have certain rules, certain regulations, certain orders in council, with regard to the entry of immigrants into this country. There are three classes of people who can come into this country to-day and I will tell you what they are. One is the farmer class. There is no protection for the poor farmer; anyone can come in and enter into competition with him.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a shame. The next
class is the farm labourer; and the third class is the female domestic servant. Eliminating for the moment the farmer-even with all his faults we love him still; everyone likes the fanner, he works while we sleep- we now have two classes-farm hand and female domestic-the man servant and the maid servant; those are the only strangers that are permitted within our gates. We brought in 48,000 maid servants last year at the time when we were losing to the United States 200,000 Canadian-born, who could employ them. Why did we bring in 48,000 maid servants?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
pretend to tell us that those people going to the United States were all able to employ other immigrants coming into this country?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I shall have to look
up the statistics on that question because I have not got the information. Now, why was there such a strong demand for domestic help and for farm hands last year in the country? I do not know that there was any
particularly strong demand for them except that these two classes of labour are not unionized; the walking delegate, the president of the Trades and Labour Council, and the workers' associations are not interested in these classes of labour. So these two classes were permitted to come freely into the country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question which is in the interest of . accuracy? He states there are only three classes allowed to come in-the farmer, the farm labourer and the female domestic servant?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that, so far as the British Isles are concerned, there are no restrictions of any kind with regard to occupation?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, that is true; but I was talking of Europe generally. A change was made last year with regard to people from the British Isles; they come in without that restriction. The streets of London-Trafalgar Square and the embankment-can be emptied into the Dominion and nothing will be said because those immigrants are British citizens -" civis Britannicus sum ". But no other class can come in except under the restrictions I have stated. Not one person from the continent of Europe can enter without a permit unless he comes under one of the three classes mentioned. Now, why should we adopt the same attitude with regard to immigration that the United States has adopted? They say, "We have too many people in this country, we do not want any more.'' Surely we cannot urge that. The United States is suffering, if I may use another medical expression, from high blood pressure; we are suffering from pernicious anaemia. And yet we are taking the same medicine that they take. I made a calculation a few daj's ago in regard to what I thought would be a reasonable number of people who could be permitted to come into the country by this form of immigration, and I thought that about five per cent would be a reasonable number per annum-that is to say one hundred people in this country ought to be able to absorb five people. I know of instances in the past where we have been easily able to absorb five per cent.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You grant quite a big
appetite to anaemic people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have got to feed
anaemic people with rich red food; and I
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.

think five per cent is what they can absorb without getting dyspepsia. Five per cent is not an unreasonable number. Now, five per cent of the population we have here is 450,000 people a year. We got in last year
140,000	of the classes that I have referred to.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The year before last
somewhat less.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I think somewhat less. Surely there must be something wrong in this system that the government has adopted. Why is it we are not permitted to have the open door in the matter of immigration into this country? I would think that was exactly what the railroads would want in order to make them pay. Perhaps I would not have advocated this drastic scheme for the amalgamation of the two lines under private ownership if we were getting people in who could support two or three lines. Sir Henry Thornton, speaking in Montreal the other day as president of the Canadian National Railways, said: "I would permit to come into this country every healthy Caucasian". And he added: "I believe that is what this country needs in order to make it prosperous." My right bon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is on record as having said that when his party .comes into power he would permit every healthy white person to enter Canada without let or hindrance. That seems to be the view of public men throughout this land-to allow every person to come in here and work out his own destiny.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have looked up the
statement to which my hon. friend referred and there was a qualification as to being capable of carrying on a useful occupation in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I would assume that.
The government said:	We are oyer-industrialized; we want more farmers, we want less industrials. Whether it is because they expect continued support from our farmer friends in the future or not I cannot say. The fact remains, however, that they are rather favourable to the entry of farmers, and they set their face strongly against any movement to the cities. Now, last year when I was speaking on this very question I made the point-at least I strove to-that if you bring in a large number of people of one class, and you bring in none of another class, the tendency will be for a levelling-up in due course; that is to say if you send people on the farm and you find that there is a lack or dearth of people in the cities the attraction to the city by means of larger wages will
I Mr. Jacobs.]
denude the farms exactly in the same way as before those people came. You must have people in the cities to attend to the wants of the industrial class, and you must have people on the farms to attend to the needs of the agricultural class. But this lop-sided policy will never be a success. Immigration must proceed in natural channels and as soon as you begin to adopt artificial schemes and artificial tricks to accomplish this or that you are interfering with nature and bound to come a cropper. For the last seven or eight years in this House I have delivered my annual on the question of immigration, and as I have said before, I have been a voice crying in the wilderness. There is no one to give me support on this question in this Chamber. I am in a class by myself. I have promised my support to any party in this House or any p-arty outside of the House who wants to get in, who will give their adhesion to a policy of this kind, and so far no one has come forward. The only member who at all approaches my view in this respect is my _ right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. I do not know whether it is a case of:
The devil was sick, the devil a monk would be;
The devil was well, the devil a monk was he.
The fact remains that when he was in power for a number of years nothing was done. The present rules and orders in council and regulations are those which were put into effect during his regime.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We were bringing our
soldiers back, and we had to absorb our soldiers then.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend
has some pretext, but the bald fact remains that he was in power and could have done something in the matter of stimulating immigration, but did nothing. Now he is prepared to do something. Whatever man hath will he give for his political life. I am rather dubious of these death-bed repentances, although I have very little choice. I know that the party in power at the present time are not prepared to do anything, although I give them my support. I have threatened and urged and gone almost beyond the limits of endurance, but so far nothing has been done, and, so far as I can see, nothing is going to be done. Now what am I to do under the circumstances?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Come across.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Keep going.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have held out the olive
branch to the hon. leader of the Progressive

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.
party, (Mr. Forke). I am willing to follow him. I am willing to follow the Labour party, small though it be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or the Ginger group.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the Ginger group. I
am willing even to take ginger.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go out and buy a farm.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So far nothing has been
done. I warn my hon. friends on this side of the House that an election is impending, that there are large numbers of people in this country who think as I do on this question and they are going to give their support to the party who will promise the open door in the matter of immigration. As for me, I have always given my support, such as it was, to the party now in power, but this matter of immigration is one which transcends politics, political .affiliations and party friendships. I always will while in this House advocate the open door in the matter of immigration, because I feel it is in the interests of the country that we should have a proper immigration policy. It is detrimental to the country to have the policy which is now in vogue, which has been handed down to us as a heritage from the right hon. leader of the opposition-a sort of Trojan, horse. We have gone along and have not examined into it to see what it was. In view of the serious condition in which the country finds itself in regard to the railway problem, in view of the appalling debt which we have on our shoulders, in view of the emigration to the States, surely the government ought to get together to see if something cannot be done in order to stimulate immigration. Something should be done by those who are leading this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend says he is in favour of the open door. Does he mean exactly what he says?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am in favour of the open door as expressed by the right hon. leader of the gentleman who has just spoken. I am in favour of allowing into the country every healths'- white person who is able to make a living. Why should not such a man be allowed to come into the country? He is going to help pay our debts, and surely he is about the most welcome person we can get just now.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the policy of the present government along that line?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The policy of the present
government on immigration is like the wisdom of God, it surpasseth all understanding. Sir Henry Thornton in his annual report thought this matter of immigration very important.
The policy of the government puts Sir Henry Thornton in a very awkward and anomalous position at the present moment. He is asked to run the railway and make it pay, and yet the door is closed to people who would come in and make it pay. He is asked, as my ancestors in Egypt were asked, to make bricks without straw, and he cannot do it. He has always been at variance with the government on this question. We have on the board of the Canadian National Railway, Mr. Tom Moore, president of Trades and Labour Councils, who has declared himself in favour of the policy, if I may call it such, which the government has now in force. He is against bringing into the country people who might compete with the .people who pay their annual dues for his upkeep. The government, evidently feeling that he was a man after their own heart, promptly made him a director of the Canadian National Railways. Now he is advocating on his side keeping out all immigrants because they are inimical to the interests of organized labour of this country. On the other hand, we find Sir Henry Thornton makes the following statement:
From time to time, and particularly during the past two years, reference has been made on various occasions to the need for immigration. The whole future of Canada and of the railway systems in Canada depends upon increased population and upon the increased traffic which would result therefrom. As compared with what might be done in order to bring about the desired result, the efforts made in the past might be termed somewhat spasmodic and unorganized. If there is to be real success the matter will have to be handled otherwise in the future. The Dominion as a whole, the provinces individuality, the railways and all other business organizations are, each of them, interested. The problem is of sufficient magnitude and importance to justify in its solution the employment of the most capable and energetic minds in the Dominion. The investment of money on a larger scale than in the past will also be required.
I call particular attention to the final paragraph which says:
The matter might be entrusted to a permanent commission constituted somewhat on the lines of the Board of Railway Commissioners, except that more commissioners would doubtless have to be appointed; and this Immigration Commission would have to be authorized to make expenditures under a general programme approved by parliament.
He says this matter is so important that a commission ought to be appointed to deal with the entire question, to make the expenditures and study the whole matter. He would favour a commission similar to the railway commission. At the present moment we have not even a standing committee in the House to deal with immigration. We have a standing committee to deal with onions and cabbages, and a standing commit-
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs.

tee to deal with fish, but when it comes to human beings, a matter in which every person in the country is interested, and with which the whole future of the country is concerned, we have nobody to whom we can refer any question at all. Surely this matter is of sufficient importance to provoke at least some interesting discussion in this House. For nineteen days, ever since this debate started, I have waited in vain to hear some public man rise in this chamber and advocate some kind of immigration policy. But nothing has been done, and feeling that nothing would be said during the entire debate, I felt it my duty to rise and make these remarks, some of which, to a certain extent, are distasteful to me to make.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member be
good enough to tell the House whether hf has any work in .Canada for the 450,000 people whom he thinks we could profitably bring in each year?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Work was found for the
hen. member for Macleod when he came, was there not?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I had the honour to be born in this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Work was found for the
hon. member when he was born.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I had to go out and look
for a job.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The 450,000 people who
should come in will be glad to go out and look for work too. This country has not been scratched yet with regard to its resources. We have the greatest natural resources in the world. We have power which, when developed, will produce, according to statistics, 41,000,000 horse-power. I notice my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) is a little surprised at the figure. I have the figures and I will go so far as to say that there is 41.200,000 horse-power waiting to be developed. We have the greatest mines in the world. We have a country larger than the United States. At the present time we have three human beings to every two square miles of territory, and yet my hon. friend says there would not be work found for
450.000	people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we have such great
possibilities of work, why cannot we put the
60.000	unemployed at work now?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend
whyu I do not know who those 60,000 people are, but I will venture to tell my

Iron, friend that most of those people are from the British Isles, gentlemen who largely do not want work. I do not say that is true of all of them, but it is true of a very large number. The hon. gentleman probably remembers the story of two Englishmen on the streets of Toronto. They were walking down Yonge street and one said to the other: "See how happy everybody looks in this city." The other said: "Why should they not be happy? Do we not own them?" That is the view the Englishman has of Canada. He will not work himself; he wants the other fellow to do the work. The men who work in this country are the men who come from the continent of Europe and not those who come from the streets of Glasgow, Liverpool and London. They are victims of the dole. They have never done any work or wanted to do it. They are wastrels, useless, and they never should be permitted to come into this country. I am speaking, of course, of a certain type. The House will not, for a moment, think I am making an attack on the British people. I say this is true of a certain type. If you will analyse each and every one of these cases, you will find that many had an opportunity to go to work, but would not go. WTe see them in our country and in other places. Every man who comes to this country and who is ready and willing to work, can find work to do. That is why those people who come from continental Europe, ignorant of our language and of our customs, are able to find work. They are willing to put their hands to anything. That is why they are a better element in the community than those whose only qualification is that- they can talk English and think they own this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
contend that the same rule applies to the Canadian-born who, as the hon. member said, were leaving Canada in large numbers and who, as he himself stated, were a better class of citizens than the foreigners we might bring in

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether my
hon. friend was here when I said that those Canadian-born people are attracted by larger wages in the United States and by the lure of the gas light, the moving picture houses and everything that is implied in a large city in the United1 States. Many of them go off the farms. I venture to say that, perhaps, 50 per cent of those people who have gone to the United States have gone off the farms in order to improve their condition in that country, not because they could not get a living

The Budget-Mr. Gould.
here. I will not believe work cannot be got in Canada, a country of 3,000,000 square miles, larger than the United States, and with 9,000,000 people. It is absurd to think people cannot get work here. In Montreal I think one man in a thousand was out of work during the winter which has just passed. That is a negligible quantity. There is plenty of work for people to do.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
mean to say that only five or six or seven hundred people were out of work in Montreal?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At most, only one person
out of one thousand people was out of work in Montreal at any one time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where did the hon.
gentleman get those figures?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I got them from a source
which, perhaps, the right hon. gentleman will not think accurate, the Montreal Star. I am afraid I have already taken up too much of the time of this House and there is nothing more that I wish to say. I did not expect to speak for more than fifteen or twenty minutes, but it is only because I had something to say that I rose to speak, strange to say.
I trust, however, my views, such as they are, will foe taken into the serious consideration of the gentlemen who now form the government of Canada. I wish to make no threats, to utter no warnings; but I cannot give my support to any party in this House that is not prepared to accept my policy as outlined to-day with regard to immigration, and I. am prepared to give my support to any party in this House that is ready to adopt this policy.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know, but I
am pretty nearly a convert to my hon. friend's idea of immigration. I would like him to answer one question in connection with it before I decide to embark on the idea. How is he going to overcome the difficulty that arises when the cities have a fixed price for carrying out the services of their people and -when, in all the rural districts of this country, we have to compete for labour and whatever our products will bring? How are you going to hold people in this vast area of country where we have unorganized labour, when the cities are holding out inducements of big pay and short hours? Can the hon. member suggest how to overcome that difficulty?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not
clearly understood my hon. friend. Would he mind repeating his question?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Organized labour and
the government are fixing remuneration in the
cities with big pay and short hours for the people who work there. In the rural districts where we have not organized labour, even the government refuses to pay to people working there the same remuneration it pays to people in the cities. How are you going to prevent immigrants from going where they can get short hours and big pay?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How are you going to prevent a farmer from selling his farm, or a hired man from going to the city? They are going there now to take the place of others. The high wages are an attraction to them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what the hon. member said. How are you going to stop that?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My theory was to allow the people to go wherever they want to go. If they want to go on the farms, let them go there; if they want to go to the cities, let them go there. If they find they cannot make a living in the cities, they will wander on to the farms. If they find they are not fitted for farming, they will go elsewhere. We have a continent to fill up. Surely it offers possibilities to every person who comes in. The man who is not a success as a farmer may become a member of parliament.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What
does this new party stand for? Does it want an overflow of population into this country for no other reason, as it seems to me, than to have a surplus of labour with a view to cutting down wages? And will that party be called the Jacobs party?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The original Jacob had only twelve sons and he went to Egypt and was a success there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish
to join with hon. gentlemen and with the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in expressing my regret at the absence through illness of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). And I think thait one new note may be introduced at this time when I say that I extend to you, Mr. Speaker, my sympathy in that the House has so long refrained from allowing you to resolve it into committee of Ways and Means. Largely that fault must be laid at the door of the government. During the past week they have been revivified and have now decided to enter into the full spirit of debate. Considerable difference is evident now in the demeanour of the House and in its activities compared with what was apparent earlier in the session when we were advised, very nearly twice a day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King),- that we
The Budget-Mr. Gould.

should do all we could to expedite the business of parliament.
I wish first of all to offer a remark or two with regard to the address delivered yesterday-afternoon by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler). That very, very dry address was delivered ostensibly for the purpose, or at least for the intended purpose, of clarifying the budget speech of the Acting Minister of Finance, and the hon. member this year appears in a different role from the one he played last year. Last year he was critical of the government and denounced them roundly because they did not make a clear exposition of the financial condition of Canada. I have here the volume of Hansard containing the remarks of the hon. gentleman at that time, and perhaps it would show better than anything else the changed attitude of the hon. gentleman if I read a few extracts from that speech of his. As I say, he was critical of the government last year; yesterday he appeared in the role of an apologist for them. He seemed to labour a point yesterday. And, in passing, let me say that I hope the fortunes of war will never permit him to have an opportunity of placing figures before this parliament in an official capacity for the House to digest, for his explanation yesterday was more confounded, it was ten times more complicated, when he got through, than was the original state of affairs which he undertook to elucidate. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman might have saved a good deal of time and might have explained the situation fully by stating that the executive of the government, who usually prepare the budget speech, have brought down this year a form of statement similar f^o that which has been followed in connection with the last seven budget speeches to which he referred, as submitted by the four preceding ministers of finance of Canada. That would have been an ample explanation of his point and it would have obviated a speech of two and a half hours. Let me now refer the House to page 1571 of Hansard of last year containing the remarks of the hon. gentleman at that time:
As a matter of fact, to give the people the idea that the day of abounding surpluses has arrived is merely to encourage spending and a lack of economy, and I therefore ask, Sir, with all due respect, if we do give the people that idea, is it the right idea to put forward? Why should we not, as a matter of fact, take the people entirely into our confidence? Why should we not exhibit to them a simple statement of our financial affairs in language which they can all understand ?
Further down the page the hon. member is reported thus:

I know that a certain part of the railway debt is at present merged in the consolidated debt; other parts are .not so merged. But it does not matter under what account the parts not so merged are taken, the parts, wherever they may be, constitute the total debt of the Dominion of Canada. In other words, we cannot increase our railway debt, without increasing our total debt.
That is the attitude which the critics of the government this year have universally taken; it is the same attitude which the hon. member for St. Lawremce-St. George took last year in his speech on the budget. This year the 'hon. gentleman has altered his position. There is another extract from the hon. gentleman's speech to which I may Tefer the House:
This government, as I have stated before and can only repeat to-day, has had to bear great expenditures, partly due to the war and partly due to causes over which they have absolutely no control. But what I venture to ask,-and I do it with a]l respect-is: Why try to place before the public a difficult system of accounting which the public itself cannot be expected to understand? Why not place before the public the actual condition of receipts and expenditures as they may occur from year to year, taking the public into our confidence as questions arise, and asking the pubiic to assist us in governing this country which is so exceedingly difficult to govern?
If hon. gentlemen wish to follow Hansard of last year further they will find in the hon. gentleman's speech a substantial en-dorsation of the comment I have made, that whereas he appeared as a critic of the government at that time he now comes forward as an apologist in their behalf.
I must say that I have never approached the task of making a speech on the budget in this House with so little cheer or with so little of what one might call vim as I do this year. And this is due to the fact that the budget on this occasion necessitates vain repetition; all the scoldings of the past must be reiterated and all the advice which hon. members have tendered the government from time to time must be offered again. It becomes discouraging therefore when individual members of parliament who have received what they regard as matured advice from their constituents find this advice discarded by the government, more particularly when gentlemen who repose in the seats of power were elected to office on the strength of the very things which their critics now advocate. I wish to refer to the visit which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his party made to western Canada last fall. I took the pleasurable opportunity of attending one of his meetings, although I had to drive the car a hundred miles either way to be present, seeing that our railway facilities are not adequate enough to enable us to take ad-

The Budget-Mr. Gould.
vantage of such occasions. We might hope for better facilities in western Canada, for at such times we have to suffer inconveniences, driving our cars hundreds of miles, to do honour to the Prime Minister of Canada. The burden of the right hon. gentleman's plea was that the people of the west had made a mistake in not having sent to Ottawa representatives who could sit in the party caucus and thereby make known to the government -what their wants were. The Prime Minister does not understand the spirit of the western people. There was very little applause when he made that statement, and it was urged continuously.
The people of the west are not to be caught with that sort of bait. The government know full well that after considerable discussion those papole had prepared a platform which they considered a new national policy for the Dominion of Canada. That was known as the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, a council which did represent people from all parts of Canada. Later on the title was changed to "The Farmers' Platform." That was a change to which I have never subscribed, and it has given much opportunity for critics of the new national policy, as we designed it to be, to misrepresent our movement as a class movement. Now I want to draw attention to this fact to prove that the people do not need to have their representatives in a government caucus or any other party caucus to make known what they are asking for, because in 1916 our platform was published, and in 1917 we find that the party now in power made another unsuccessful attempt at the polls, and then it was that they appeared to suddenly realize that a national convention was necessary. It was held in this city in 1919, and a platform was evolved which bears many close resemblances to the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. Evidently someone was aware either of what the people required or that another platform had been built which would appeal to the country. I have heard, and hon. gentlemen here have heard it declared, a thousand times, that there is similarity in the two platforms, that there is no reason why the Progressive party should be distinct and apart from the Liberal party. Well, in so far as their platforms go I admit that they have much in common. But while I admit that, I have also to draw the attention of the House and the country to the fact that we were the originators of the very meritorious platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture.
That is my first proof that the people do not need to be represented in a party caucus to make known their wishes. My second proof is this, and I might be allowed to illustrate it. We of western Canada look upon the party politics of the Maritime provinces almost as if it was a disease. I believe that no more bitter political fights have ever been waged in Canada than those which have characterized elections in the Maritime provinces. Even since this parliament was brought into being we have heard many times about the "solid sixteen" from Nova Seotia, and we know something of the partisan spirit that distinguishes the politics of the Mari-times. I do not say that harshly, but the fact that the " solid sixteen " have sat in the party caucuses continuously and the fact that we have heard louder murmurings from the Maritimes during the past two or three years than from any other part of Canada shows the futility of the party caucus to satisfy the wants of the people. If representation in a party caucus is a means whereby remedies may be initiated, why do we hear these constant murmurings from the Maritime provinces? I have thought that hon. members from the Maritime provinces, as representing the needs and rights of their constituents, have so much in common with the representatives of the people of western Canada, that if they would stand in their places and openly denounce and vote against the administration which they now support, their constituents in the Maritimes would rally to their support. And I am not speaking now of any one particular party; my remarks are applicable to the two old parties. I am sure the people down there would back up any of their representatives who would take that course. It is my opinion that the people of the Maritime provinces and the people of the west have so much in common that, combined, we could make industrial Canada sit up and take notice.
I give it again. Sir, as my opinion that industrial Canada has been the cause of three-fourths of the political and economic unrest in the Dominion since 1874. We are paying a huge price-we always have-for the erection and the continuation of industrial Canada. We are asked to continue it now. If we had the condition -which I have pictured, we would have factories going to the coal areas of Nova Scotia and of Alberta. Instead of that, under our present policy we subsidize the coal barons-and tax ourselves-to take coal to the industrial area, and in turn that industrial area manufactures products upon which we protect them and again fine our-
2372 .
The Budget-Mr. Gould.

selves. In a word, under our present policy we levy a double fine upon the people. As I said before, we should force these factories to locate in our coal fields rather than penalize ourselves by subsidizing them to bring coal to the industrial area. By so doing they would have a growing market in western Canada for agricultural implements, and we would save freight both on coal and on implements. This is applicable to the Maritime provinces, it is likewise applicable to western Canada. Perhaps our condition at the present time is a judgment upon us because of our blind partisan attitude in the past.
I wish to refer to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), not in any unkind spirit at all, and I regret that he is not in hie seat. There is a personal something that binds the hon. member for Brome and the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) in a tie for friendship. It commenced in 1919, when he, accompanied by another hon. member, visited the electoral district of Assiniboia, and took an active part in a certain by-election. It was at that time that I made the hon. gentleman's acquaintance. Fresh from the convention halls of the city of Ottawa, where the Liberal platform of 1919 was framed and adopted, he proclaimed to the people the following: Here is our new platform, here is the Liberal party's pledge to put this platform into execution, all you need do is to entrust to then} the reins of office, and I pledge my word that that platform will be put into effect; you do not need any other representative than a Liberal. Well, the reply of the people of Assiniboia was that they had been deceived before, and they did not propose to be deceived again. I would' ask the hon. member for Brome, who was right? In the course of a very able address delivered by the hon. member some few nights ago, he laid down the policies which he thought Canada should follow. I am in accord with him very near to the limit, but When he added tnat he could not oppose the budget because he feared the government would be defeated, I felt I must part company with him.
We have contended, Sir, many, many times
and we would not make the contention if we did not have ample justification for it- that there is not the difference, really, of the snap of the fingers between the two old political parties of this country, the Liberals and the Conservatives. This view is confirmed in the policies of both parties-not as enunciated but as practised. A proposal which is before the House and the country to-day is another illustration of the similarity of our two old friends-I refer to the proposed tariff board I can quite believe that if this becomes an 
issue they will quarrel and squabble over it for weeks in this House as to who shall constitute that tariff board, but the main principle of the board is already in the minds of the government as it is also in the minds of the official opposition. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has his resolution on the order paper, and he proclaims that this tariff board is going to be erected to look into the evils that beset us. Before I make a few remarks upon that, I want to refer to a conclusion I reached after reading an article in the Financial Post of April 17 in which the experiences are- given of a gentleman named Mr. Beld-i.ng, who had been delegated by certain newspapers in the province -of New Brunswick to go to western Canada and declare unto them the difficulties under which the Mari-times were labouring. As he expressed it himself, he went forth proclaiming the policies of the Maritimes and the things that would benefit them, but he came back making a d;fferent kind of speech. Summing up, he stated that he thought the solution for the economic difficulties under which Canada was labouring might be foundl if the- country were divided into four zones and each of these zones sent representatives to a conference and there, through compromise and otherwise, an endeavour were made to reach a solution that would be acceptable to all parts of the country. That, in my opinion, would be much better than a tariff board; it would help to solve the problem. I do not wholly agree with Mr. Belding's conclusions. He says that the various zones should be represented by delegates from the boards of trade of all the zones referred to. I wondered as I read the article whether he knew that there was an industry in Canada called agriculture, which represents at least fifty-two per cent of the population and seventy-five per cent of the created wealth of the country. I wondered why he should confine it to boards of trade; his urban mind seemed to think there was nothing else in Canada but boards of trade. Agriculture has large organizations representative of that phase of our national life, organizations that are paying attention as best they can to the economic difficulties of Canada. I do not condemn the principle that Mr. Belding has advanced, but I do want him to appreciate the fact that agriculture will not stand aside and allow boards of trade to dictate a policy for the Dominion of Canada.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

The Budget-Mr. Gould.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext: This book states so, and the argument I am trying to make is that when our Conservative friends charge our Liberal friends with being the cause of the closing down of the factories and the men being out of work as a result of the paltry reductions of last year, why did they not say, ''We reduced the tariff to a greater extent and consequently we must also have closed the factories and put men out of work"?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) I would say that if the paltry tariff reductions the government made in the tariff brought about such disastrous results, then the Conservatives should have brought about a more serious condition, because they made greater tariff reductions, although they claimed to be a high tariff party.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong so far as I or this party are concerned. We never advertised that we were going to introduce a high tariff at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, that is all right. I will accept the statement of the hon. gen'.leman, if that is satisfactory. But the people of Canada believed that my hon. friends ad-
The Budget-Mr. Gould.

vertised it in that way, and I think :f hon. members will read' the propaganda which follows in the same Liberal-Conservative handbook, they will see that it is advocated there, when they are appealing to the different classes of people, particularly in the urban centres.
I wish to refer to the resolution which the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has placed upon the order paper, which he has not had an opportunity to debate. There hon. members will find the argument for a consistent and even a higher tariff. The inference is given that the tariff has to be raised to give more work and more employment for the workman. We want to have a policy in this country, whether it is a Liberal or Conservative policy, that the people can depend upon. If you elect one party which profess a lower tariff, let them cany out that policy and give a lower tariff.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not remember the handbook my hon. friend speaks of, but I presume what the Conservative party were setting forth at that time was what they had done for the farming community in this country, and were not advocating a lower tariff. They were pointing out that they had made cuts in agricultural implements which should satisfy the farmer, but they got very little support from the farmers of the prairie provinces.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend again, I was not endeavouring to prove the merits of the high or the low tariff at the present time. I was trying to prove the inconsistencies of the two old political parties in this country, and also endeavouring to prove that there is such a similarity in practice that the people do not need to take their assertions very seriously.
Now there are two points brought forth in the proposed' resolution of the right hon. leader of the opposition, and the first one is that the farmer is to be at last included in the principle of protection. Always in the past those who talked protection aimed at the farmer as a victim. At the present time, since the farmer has risen to his feet and protests because he has been made in the past the victim, this sop is held out to him in the hope that it will beguile him fiirthe". Let me assure Lon. members that he is not going to be beguiled, because he realizes that there is only a certain amount of wealth created and although it is said to be distributed equally, he knows that those who have been the recipients of special favours will continue to receive the benefit and the farmer will get the small share in the end.

The second point is this, that the resolution proposes that a commission shall find out and report back to the government whenever abuse is made of the taxes. That is very enlightening, because we had all been given to understand-and I am sure the speeches that have been made in this chamber will bear me out in that statement-that it never was considered that those industries that had been the recipients of special privileges ever took advantage of that fact or did a wrong thing. If the right hon. leader of the opposition were in his place I should like to ask him wherein and when he found that any of these industries had taken advantage of the tariff. That is information we have had ever since we have been purchasing implements, and yet the right hon. leader of the opposition, the champion of higher protection in this country, has just proclaimed to the world that at last he has found out that some of these industries have been taking advantage of the tariff. It is very enlightening indeed.
Now, Sir, I give it as my opinion that if a tariff commission were appointed to look into the merits of the case, I would only support it on the understanding-and it is a theory which I have advanced at least half a dozen times in this chamber-that the commission should be empowered to go in and ascertain the merits of the institution which asks for protection. That is to say, a commission should be delegated or empowered to go to these organizations who think they have a right to have this special privilege, who have accepted it in the past, who have been guilty of malpractices as the right hon. leader of the opposition states in his resolution, and investigate these concerns. That is the first and the only thing I would delegate to theim and they should be asked to bring in a report to this House. I should want to know how the physical value of their plants compared with the fictitious values which we have been led to believe they possess. At least, if the values were fictitious we would find it out. They would report to the House and we could apply a scientific adjustment to the statements made in the report and find out how they stood. We have had our doubts in the past and made representations, and yet no government in Canada from the time protection was first imposed has had the courage to appoint a commission and send that commission to the industries to ascertain from them the reasons why they asked for this protection. It has been very interesting, Mr. Speaker, from time to time to hear the gratuitous advice that has been tendered by the proponents of high protection,

The Budget-Mr. Gould.
yea, even to the Mother Country, Hon. gentlemen can bear me out in this, that sometimes it has almost reached the point where they would ridicule the fiscal policy -of the Mother Country. With that in view, I made a clipping from a paper, and I want our Conservative friends to pay particular attention to this, because these words come from the mouth of a member of the British House of Commons. The report is headed, " The path of protection," it is applicable to my argument, it expresses exactly my views and the views of scores of thousands of the workers of Canada and it is just as applicable to the people of Canada as to any country in the world where the .principle of protection is in force. These remarks were made by Captain Wedgewood Benn, DjS.O., Liberal in the British House of Commons:
The Path of Protection
Captain Wedgwood Benn, D.S.O., Liberal, in British House of Commons:
I am speaking about the lobbies of this House, and I am referring to the change that has come over our political campaigns in connection with this sort of debate and this sort of duty. We are constantly being pressed by people who come here not for grievances to be redressed, not for some public interest to be attended to, but because they want something done which will put money in their pockets. Men who in the old days thought of nothing but their customers and pleasing their customers think now of nothing but wheedling members of Parliament and nobbling Ministers. People, who in the old days thought that the secret of success was to give better value for money, say to-day, "If we can get a tariff, better value is of no account." Their object is not to promote the public interest but to manipulate divisions in the House of Commons.
That is a complete change, and a very evil feature. I cannot summarize this point better than in the words of a Tory of Tories, the Noble Lord who sits for the University of Oxford (Lord Hugh Cecil), who said: "Protection will lead to the corruption of our public life as it has led to the corruption of the life of other countries The purity of our public life is the lifeblood of Europe. If Conservatives go in for Protection, I will have nothing to do with such an apostate party. If they determine to travel down the path of dishonor and Imperial ruin, I will wash my hands clean of so great a crime.
That is the -condemnation. That is the answer to hon. members who may think it their right or duty to challenge the fiscal policy of Great Britain.
A tariff -lias the same effect as a depreciated currency. That is to say, if you impose a 10 per cent tariff tax, the purchasing power of the individual is decreased by that 10 per cent. If you impose a 20 per cent tariff tax, the purchasing power of the in-ddividual is decreased exactly one-fifth. If you impose a 25 per cent tariff tax, the purchasing power of the individual is decreased one-quarter. We have had a condition similar to that in Canada, and it means one-quarter less purchasing power or one-quarter less need for the beneficiary to exert himself. Let me illustrate and this may be used in reply to the charges of our hon. friends that men are out of work. About twelve years ago-and I use my own case as an illustration,-I purchased a Massey-Harris five-foot mower for the sum of $65, giving my note for it. It was a good machine and I still have it working on my farm. Last year when I went home I required another mower, and I went to the HasseyvHarris agent and said:	"I want another five-foot mower. What is the price?" He told me it was $112. I said: "But I ha-e just returned from Ottawa and we had a cut in the tariff on these mowers this year". He said:	"I will look that up". In the tariff
and the sales tax the reduction was $5 and I paid him $107 cash for the mower, taking it home. I -had saved $5, but I turned around and said: "Now I want a scrub scythe", and I got it for 85. Did the worker have any less work to do because I bought two implements with the same money, or would he have had less had I just purchased one? That is by way of illustration.
I propose now to direct the attention of the House to the practical views which reveal themselves in the budget. The first thing which stands out so that he who reads may understand, is the fact that we have a national debt of $2,431,487,112.88. In conversation with a gentleman to-day I was using the figure of 9,700,000 as the population of Canada. He said: "Man,, you are away out. I would not mind betting, if it could be proved, that the population of Canada is not more than 7,000,000 to-day." The item, however, was made up as of March 31, 1924, of $2,417,783,274.88, to which is added in 1924, according to the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), a deficit of $13,703,838, making the total which I gave before. Taking the population at 9,700.000 souls, we find that makes a per capita debt of $2,506.70. I have an object in giving those figures, and that is to bring home to- the people of Canada, if I possibly can, the exact position by which the are surrounded, the burden that they have upon their shoulders. Possibly, this will be an incentive to the people to pay more attention to the affairs of state and to see that real cause shall be shown before any individual shall come back to this House. An average family of five would be assuming a burden of federal debt of $12,533.50; or a family of nine, that is seven children and the two parents-and I know a home not far from mine where there are nine-would be assuming a burden of federal debt of
The Budget-Mr. Gould.

$22,560.30. These are practical figures that the layman can understand. The charge cannot be placed against them that was made across the floor of this House in regard to the budget.

I am aware of that and
I will prove later that a great proportion of

it was due to expenditures on railways which were built thirty years ahead of their time. That is the maladministration to which I refer and it is all included in the national debt. subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But my hon. friend said it was all due to this government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I say that the Acting Minister of Finance brought down figures to show that there was a deficit of $830,000,000; that is to say, we have a total amount involved in connection with the Canadian National Railways of over $2,000,000,000. But while we have lines of steel and the rolling stock of subsidiary concerns to offset that, th e government in my opinion brings down a statement showing a total slippage in earnings of $830,000,000.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think that it was a mistaken policy to take over and consolidate these railways?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not at all. Indeed1, as far back as 1910 and 1911 the whole cry in western Canada was that such a consolidation was bound to come about because the people of the west were strongly condemning the principles that had obtained in connection with our railway policies in Canada up to that time. Hon. gentlemen in this House will bear me out that the firm opinion in western Canada at that time was that the principle of national ownership of our railways would inevitably be recognized and adopted for the reason that the method that

The Budget-Mr. Gould,
had been pursued by the political parties had so far been disadvantageous to the country. Now that the hon. gentleman has put that question to me I want to assure him that I do not for a moment attack the principle of government ownership of our railways. I will say however that this principle has not been really tried in Canada; and that statement might be advanced by way of reply to the hon. member who spoke this afternoon (Mr. Jacobs). That hon. gentlemen condemns the principle of national ownership, but I repeat that it has never been fairly tried in this country, and I honestly believe that if it were given a reasonable test on an equal basis with the Canadian Pacific Railway it would prove that the Canadian National railway system could be just as successfully operated. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that to-day, with the heavy extra burden which the Canadian National Railways must carry, they are making a wonderful showing and are compelling the Canadian Pacific to do better than perhaps tnev would otherwise do.
How we are to save Canada in the present crisis is perhaps a difficult question to settle. The present government is trying to save it by scrapping its 1919 platform, while our Conservative friends propose to put the country on its feet by making the cost of living higher than it is at the present time.

speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman
must have been out of his seat when I gave figures to prove that the Conservative party had reduced the duty on agricultural implements to a greater extent than the Liberal party had done, so that the cry of closed factories was more applicable as against our Conservative friends than as against the Liberals. Now, there is another thought that occurs to me in connection with our railways, and that is that every dollar of their capitalization can be shown on paper. Such is not the case with the Canadian Pacific Railway. When making comparisons we must bear in mind that in cash, in dollars and cents, the capitalization of our National Railways can all be set down in black and white; on the other hand, there cannot be shown on paper everything that the Canadian Pacific Railway has received. For instance, the lands given to the Canadian Pacific were acquired by that company at a dollar an acre, and they say that this land to-day is worth fifteen, eighteen, twenty-five and thirty dollars, these enchanced values 152
being attributable to the activities of the men who had gone in and settled on the land along the lines of the railway. These men were pioneer settlers, and hon. gentlemen must remember that they had to assess themselves municipally to build roads past the vacant sections of land which the Canadian Pacific Railway held out of use. These vacant sections were between the farms and the school, the church and the town generally and they were the breeding place of everything injurious to agriculture. And besides that they were exempt from taxation. Our Conservative friends must not forget that they are responsible for granting the charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and while I do not blame them for doing that I think at the same time that more consideration should have been given the people. If you take into consideration the amount which the people who settled around these vacant lands of the railway were obliged to assess themselves municipally to make improvements and the loss to the agriculturist because of the destructive pests these vacant lands harbored you will find that all that the Canadian Pacific Railway received, indirectly as well as directly, does not appear on paper, and if all these things were shown on paper in the case of the Canadian Pacific, even the present capitalization of the Canadian National would sink into insignificance in comparison.
Last year in the vote on the budget the government received a majority of 112, If the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr Shaw) were in his seat I would ask him to predict the majority on this occasion. The hon. member is the only prophet I know of in this House and I am sure that if he knew he would tell me; had he known I was going to speak he might have assembled his snakes and toads, with the curl of smoke, and told me beforehand what the majority might be. However, if I might venture a prediction on my own account, I would suggest that the majority this year will be much less; let us say that it will be approximately one-fifth of what it was last year. And even if the government secures one-fifth of the majority it got last year I argue that this will represent a decline in prestige to that extent owing to failure to implement its pledges. This government was elected on a platform similar to that of the Canadian Council of Agriculture which preceded it by three years. I do not want that point missed. The group opposite, elected on a platform similar to that of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, added to the members on this side who support the same policy, represent three-fourths of the membership of the House of Commons,

The Budget-Mr. Gould

and that I contend would fairly reflect the opinion of the people of Canada, particularly concerning tariff matters. But- although the government came into office on the strength of those pledges, they have now taken frighi at the hue and cry of industrial Canada; because of some picayune reductions on implements last year fear has driven the administration into retreat. They are poor champions of their policy if they allow an industrial area in Canada, representing only approximately one-fourth of the elected members of the House of Commons, to scare them into the position which we find them holding today. They are absolutely afraid to step out and carry out any of the planks of their platform.
Now. Sir, I want to refer to one or two things which appear in the budget, and particularly to the tax that is proposed on a certain document which, though not a cheque, yet represents a man's ability to go to the bank and get money. Representations have been made to the government from the floor that an enormity is being practised upon the individual who ships cream. Let me illustrate. A man who is established in the dairy business with a herd of twenty or thirty cows will get quite a large cheque for the cream that he ships to the factory, and the two cent stamp does not matter very much to him; but the poor individual who is starting in the dairy business, the soldier settler, if you will, who is possessed of only two or three or four cows, gets maybe a two and a half dollar cheque for his five-gallon can of cream, which it has taken him some time to fill; he will be obliged by this proposed legislation to pay two cents upon every cheque he receives. I say that in this regard you are taxing the poorest man, and the proposal is not equitable, it is not just, and no government should attempt to place it on the statute books, no matter what the financial needs of the country may be. I think, with other hon. members, that $10 should be the minimum cheque upon which stamp duty should be paid. I might carry the story further, I might refer members to the Turgeon report, which states positively and conclusively something which we who grow wheat knew, that the individual who is forced to sell his wheat upon the street pays the greatest price for the marketing of his product. He has to pay this two cent stamp duty on a very small cheque, whereas the more fortunate individual who ships his wheat in bulk receives his money back by express. That is where the greater part of the profits are made, at the expense of the poor individual. By last year's budget the man who

can least afford to pay has to bear this two cent stamp duty on every small cheque. I have seen a man unfortunate enough to have to take in a load of tough, damp grain for which he received a paltry sum of money. But unhappily the man who is hardest hit is up against this two cent stamp tax oftener than the man whose transactions are on a much larger scale. I think if the government knew the condition of affairs they would not endeavour to impose such a tax.
Now Mr. Speaker, I have before me a programme which I believe should be upon the statute books to-day, and I am confident that the majority of these proposals which I am about to read would have been enacted had the people reposed confidence in the Progressive party in 1921. We have urged the present administration to incorporate in our statute books the majority of these measures which I Shall now enumerate. Had we been entrusted with power we would have enacted into law the following measures:
1.	The redemption of all untaxed war bonds that remain in Canada and the imposition of a tax upon them.
2.	A Dominion system of long term credits for agriculturists, whereby they might have an opportunity by a system of amortization to pay off their debts. This is something due our agriculturists, and they will not be satisfied until such a measure is enacted. The government were aware of the conditions which called for such legislation at the time they took office, and surely they have had a sufficient interval within which to inaugurate such a policy.
3.	A commission to ascertain the actual position of those industries which ask for protection or high tariff, and also to ascertain how many of them are indigenous to Canada. I think the establishment of such a commission is long overdue.
4.	Writing down the over-capitalization of the Canadian National Railways so as to put the system on a fair basis to compete with its rival.
5.	Settlement of the natural resources question. I think we can safely say that we would have honestly attempted to bring that about.
6.	The principle of proportional representation. The government promised to bring down a bill for this purpose, but they are very lax in redeeming their promise.
7.	Revaluation of soldier settlement land and other soldier assets and placing them on a normal basis. This is due our soldier settlers, indeed overdue, but the government

The Budget- Mr. St. Pere
are lax in their duty, and make no attempt to do anything that might cause them to go down to posterity with a good name, which after all is the thing to be desired.
8.	Completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
9.	Enactment of a law that 7 per cent be the maximum interest chargeable by our banks, and the imposition of severe penalties for infractions of the law. This is another piece of legislation which the government should have enacted; certainly we would have placed such a law on the statute books.
10.	Revival of the wheat board in 1922. Yes, this was very dear to the mind of the westerner, and it does not affect anybody else.
11.	Amendment of the Bankruptcy Act to make it applicable to the agriculturist, thereby giving him a chance to start again. That is another thing due the agriculturist that this government should have enacted long ago; but no, they sit idly by and are loath to do anything.
12.	Suspension of the coastal laws thereby controlling lake freight rates. That is something we would certainly have done.
13.	Withdrawal of the 'Canadian Government Merchant Marine from the North Atlantic conference, and the use of the ships to bring down the north Atlantic freight rates.
14.	Removal of the tariff and sales tax from the necessities of life, and the imposition of a luxury tax sufficient to make up the difference.
15.	Here is another original suggestion. What would hon. members t'hink about a tax on golf courses? I would tax all except municipal golf courses. We have our millionaires with their luxurious golf clubs and extensive grounds untaxed, while hon. members in our legislatures say that the child who goes out to purchase a 25 cent movie ticket should pay a tax.
Mr. ST. PERE:	W'ould my hon. friend
tax professional hockey?

I would reduce the indemnities of members living within a few hundred 152*
miles of Ottawa. I have occupied more time than I intended, Mr. Speaker, but it will not have been wholly wasted if the government will see the wisdom of taking steps immediately to translate some of my suggestions into law and thus give the people of Canada good reason to rejoice.
Mr. E. C. ST. PERE (Hochelaga) (translation) : Mr. Speaker, "Give me a good policy and I shall give you good finances." We must admit that this parliament should not give to these words of Baron Louis too great a scope, for, in these practical times, we must conclude that good financing can be shown, even though the balance sheet shows only a small margin to the good. Agreeing with the great Gladstone, I would like to see that the yearly budget of all our governments be not too large. This would encourage our administrators in being more economical in expenditures and consequently, the country would be better governed.
I am not, Sir, a follower of the doubting apostle. I have faith in the honour, ability and in the science of those who the government appoint to the administration of public affairs, especially in those employees of our administration who have been called upon to fill the so responsible position of making up our budgets and, in particular, of compiling its very interesting statistics which we call our yearly financial report.
Mr. Speaker, I have always made it a point to be sufficiently truthful as to not lie to myself, and to contend that, at present, our country enjoys unparalleled prosperity, would be to misrepresent the facts. On the other hand neither am I a pessimist and I shall be content, together with all the practical people of this country, to point out that our public debt is very large, and I consider it a duty to endeavour, with all those who think of the future, to find measures so as to face the situation; without looking very far back to discover the causes which have brought on these conditions, causes which everybody knows, and that I do not think proper to remind the public of too often. What is or rather what are the causes of our troubles? We are no worse off, in Canada, than the people in other foreign countries. All these countries, Sir, have suffered from this great cataclysm which is called the Great war. In all those countries we find, to-day, a revival of energy, an overflow of patriotism to face the present situation, and I cannot see why, here, in Canada, we, with this youthful country filled with hopes, should fall back and confine ourselves to a narrow pessimism and think that in our beautiful country we have

speechtext: We have also heard, Sir, quite a lot about emigration. Certain speech makers would have us believe that our present tariff as the primary, the active, the sole cause why our people are going away to the United States. Such is not the ease. I am speaking more particularly of what is taking place in my own province. Certain French Canadians have a habit of migrating periodically to the United States and returning some time later. Those who are acquainted with the French-Canadian centres of New England will understand me when I say that I wonder if these people are as happy in the land of Uncle Sam as they were at home here in Canada. I have visited personally the "Little Canadas" of a number of New England cities and I make bold to declare that the French Canadians of our great cities, that all the workmen of our great cities, are far better off than those in the United States.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. ST. PERE:	Last fall I had the good
fortune to listen to a sermon, in the church of St. Louis de France, Montreal, preached by his Lordship, the venerable Bishop HallS, of Hearst. He requested the congregation of that magnificent parish to carry his words to the province of Quebec, and to say to all French Canadians: "By all means stay where you are! What I am telling you now,-said the venerable prelate-is the opinion of a great many French Canadian parish priests in New England; they have said to me: "Urge French Canadians to remain in the province of Quebec. There they are at home and they are far, far happier indeed than they can ever hope to be under the Stars and Stripes".
And since we must speak of immigration let us deal with that question.
I do not hold with the hon, member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) that we should adopt the policy of the "Open Door".

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. ST. PERE: The hon. member told us this afternoon that the United States and Canada were each afflicted with a great evil, though of a different character in each case, and he proposed to apply the same remedy to both. I am wondering if the open door, the policy upheld by my hon friend from George Etienne Cartier for eradicating this supposed Canadian evil, would really be the remedy we need. Apparently our .population is too small; we are told that we should increase our population 60 as to ensure the profitable operation of the Canadian National Railways. I maintain, Sir, that if there be something wrong with Canada we should 'be very careful
(Mr. St. Ptre.l
not to take an overdose of the medicine in attempting to right matters.
I am very close to my constituents; I meet them every day,-and the workmen of our Large cities are not only French Canadians; some are English too and Irish,-and they say to me: "Mr. St. Pere, try and get the government not to open the door too wide to immigration; we, who belong to this country, we who are Canadian-born, have first right to a living in Canada, and these foreigners come here and take our jobs away from us".
I congratulate the government for closing thi door a little, and to go one step further, until prosperity returns somewhat to the Canadian soil, I would be in favour of having this door closed a little more.	.
Let us now examine our National Railways. We have, in this House, a great number of theorists. We should have a great many practical men. I look upon this enterprise- however national it may be-as very detrimental and, mark you, I do not sanction by that a merger of the National Railways with the Canadian Pacific Railway so as to create a monopoly in Canada, but what I advocate, what the business men of my electoral division request, what the workmen cal! for, what those who possess moderate means ask, what those who, for the greater part, pay the income tax ask, is that these large expenditures be diminished. My views on this subject agree with those of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). It is all very well, under the plea of attracting traffic, to spend money on radio, and so on, however, these large outlays, this additional burden that the country is called upon to carry, where do they come from, if not from the pockets of the taxpayers of this country? And, notwithstanding all the arguments the theorists may bring to bear on this subject, notwithstanding all that may be said by those who see in this national enterprise a good business transaction, a patriotic thing, there is not a man in this House who can convince me that it is to the advantage of Canada to keep up an enterprise which threatens us with deficits for twenty-five years to come, whatever may be the figure of our population. And moreover why delude ourselves with false hopes? Will Canada, ten years hence, have 10,000,000 more of population than it has to-day? Whatever the case may be, I state that an enterprise which threatens us with a yearly deficit of $50,000,000 for fifteen years to come, is not a desirable one, and that the sooner we improve our situation, the better the population of this country will be satisfied.

The Budget- Mr. St. Pere
