subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now, Sir,
coming to immigration. I am not an extreme opponent of immigration; however I must state that this immigration should be closely watched. It is all very well, after a thorough physical inspection of the candidates, to bring into this country handsome specimens, statues of Tanagra, if you like, however there is one thing that we must closely watch: it is the mentality of those who come to us.
We have listened, this year, to various views aired in this House; we have heard the claims of those-including even a lady member- who wished at any price to amend the British North America Act; we have listened to some asking us to pay a pension to all the gunmen and burglars who ransack our homes, and we were forced to listen to long winded speeches on resolutions devoid of all practical sense. And, we afterward ask why the sessions are so long, and why the cost is so great 1 There is one suggestion which I might make to the government-and, on this subject, I must beg your indulgence if I take advantage of the privilege afforded, at present, to the members of the House, of making a long speech. I hope that in the near future, I shall see myself obliged, and this with pleasure, to cut short my remarks so that they may be summed up in a half hour speech, the practical side will perhaps be the gainer, and the country will benefit greatly from the economy which this will allow us to carry out.
Mr. Speaker, after the remarks I have just made, this House will, perhaps, want to know what are my views on the tariff. I think my views are those of a practical man; I have matured my views, Sir, after consulting the grey hair business men of my electoral division; I considered myself too young to come to a definite opinion on the subject. Here are my views on the tariff: I would put the maximum tax on the unnecessary things; this would be on a downward scale until it reached things necessary, and it would stop at the necessities of life.
I would go one step further; I am not the Finance Minister, however, if I were, perhaps, I would be bold enough to make the following suggestion: I would submit for the approval of the House, a proviso to be placed in the tariff, a flexible proviso, as the one *which, at present, regulates the American tariff. Those who reside in the neighbourhood of the great Canadian Metropolis, I might mention those from all parts of the province of Quebec, and also my colleagues from the rural constituencies, would support me on this question. I mean the early fruit and vegetables which come to us in the spring from the American gardens. I do not wish to deprive anyone, for I am against every kind of prohibition, of alcohol as well as of races, however, we must not forget that all farm products come from the United States in the spring; again do I state, I do not wish to deprive anyone of the pleasure of eating to his heart's content these products, by advocating a very high tariff, however, the moment that the same Canadian products are placed on our markets, I think it would be a sound policy so. as to help both our market gardeners and farmers, to raise somewhat the tariff on American products.

speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question? Would he be in favour of raising the Canadian tariff to the level of the American tariff on said products?

speechtext:
Quite so.
It is rumoured, Sir, that if a vote were taken, at present, throughout the country, because of the stagnation in business-for I told you, Sir, at the outset of my speech, that I was am optimist-a great number of Canadians would vote to annex Canada to the United States. I do not know where such Canadians come from, however, I take advantage of this occasion to assert-and past history is there to prove it-that if this project received a favourable vote, the majority favouring annexation of Canada to the United States would certainly not come from the beautiful province of Quebec. From an historical viewpoint we are Conservatives. Let the Americans come here and bring their capital., they will be received with open arms; if they wish to carry on their work peacefully, they are again welcome; but never will the fond hopes held, in the past, by the hon. Senator Cabot Lodge of Massachusetts materialize, he stated to one of the most prominent French-Canadians in the United States, that within twenty-five years Canada would form part of the United States and that the first to pass over to the Stars and Stripes would be the French Canadians of the province of Quebec. I think, Sir, that the hon. Senator Cabot Lodge had formed a wrong opinion of us, for if there is a people who want Canada to remain Canada, if there is a people who have at heart the love of their country and especially a faith in its future; if there is a people, I say, filled with such sentiments and desirous of seeing them survive, this people is surely that of the province
The Budget- Mr. St. Pere

of Quebec. We are blessed, Sir, with a government system without its equal in the world, and the task of all good citizens, and especially of the public man, is to adapt it to the needs of the day by modernizing practices somewhat grown old and established for an entirely different economic and social status. In accordance with this principle, it is not a new list of reforms which it is necessary to offer parties, but a technique capable of bringing about reforms. Political strife, not only necessary, but fruitful in the future, will have no other function than to eliminate the negative-unattainable-the positive constituting itself in the general consensus.
My wishes to the opposition are that it remain-as Lamartine thought it at one time -the party of hopes; 'but what I still more desire is that the policy of our government be the science, the policy of all that may help to make national life healthier, more intense and more stable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I should be congratulated or commiserated on the fact that I have been unable to follow the hon. member (Mr. St. Pere) who immediately preceded me, in the most excellent political speech he has just delivered. Fortunately I am aible to read the beautiful language in which he spoke, although I could not follow his spoken discourse; therefore he will pardon me if I do not attempt to deal with his arguments in the few remarks that I am about to make.
The gentleman who preceded him was the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) to my immediate left. While I have no desire to say very much about the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia, I would like to call attention to one or two things. In the first place he condemned the party of which I am a humble member in that during their regime they reduced the duty on agricultural implements; in other words they were the only party within his political knowledge who carried out the pledges they gave. Not only in this House but in the west, in the country from which my hon. friends or most of tnem, come, on platform alter platform they have referred to the fact that my leader when in opposition proposed to lower the duty on agricultural implements, and the present member for Assiniboia tries to condemn the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) because he was the only man who fulfilled the pledges he had made. But the hon. gentleman went further: he said that the farmer had no protection. I would like

to point out that while the protection for the farmer, especially in the province of Ontario, is entirely inadequate, there has been protection, and that protection is entirely owing to the party to which I have the honour to belong.
He said further-and I am going to get through with his remarks as quickly as possible-that a 10 per cent duty meant a 10 per cent decrease in the purchasing power of the individual and a 20 per cent duty meant a 20 per cent decrease ini the purchasing power of the individual. Why not follow that along; why not say that if we did as they have done in the United States, place a duty of 100 per cent on many articles, the result would be no purchasing power at all? The thing is absolute nonsense on the face of it.
During the course of his remarks-I called attention to it at the time-the hon. member for Assiniboia was wrong in his figures. He said! the debt per capita in Canada was something over $2,000 when as a matter of fact it is less than $300. It shows how accurate the hon. member was in the majority of his statements.
Now, I am the eightieth speaker, Sir, in this momentous debate; seventy-nine have preceded me, and I think the government side have taken their share in the debate. Hon. gentlemen opposite have referred to members of this party as pessimists. I listened very carefully to the remarks of my hon. friends, when I was in the House; the speeches of the others I have read very carefully, and I have yet to find a man either on the government side or on my left, or in this party, who is entirely satisfied with conditions as they are to-day. I have not heard one man say that he was satisfied with the budget as brought down-not one. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his address quoted more than copiously from extracts in an attempt to show that the United States were just as badly off as we were, but that does not make us any better, nor does it make the United States any worse. The greater part of the-speech of the Prime Minister, however, was directed along that line.
We have another minister, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). During his maiden address on the tariff he spent the greater part of his time in showing up what he called Conservative propaganda and in taking short extracts out of various papers-I think the longest was about three lines-to show that certain factories were going ahead, that some were going to open up, and that sort of thing. Well, I would like the Minister' of Labour-

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
because it particularly applies to his department-to go to one of our industrial towns, I do not care which one; he can take his choice of Hamilton, Brantford, my own home town of Parry Sound-and ask the man on the street what the actual conditions are. Let him ask almost any of the men in the factories down in our country who are working from two, three to four days a week, who have homes of their own, who are not able to migrate to the United States for various personal and business reasons. These are the men to ask, and I am sure that if either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour goes to the trouble of making such an inquiry of the men in the real industrial centres in Quebec or Ontario, I do not care which, he will find out the facts.
The present tariff, Mr. Speaker, is the result of what the Prime Minister has designated as a "pause." Last session he said that the government intended to pause-shall I say, in its downward path?-in its path, anyway, and that for the present there would be no material changes in the tariff. Well, if the policy suggested by the government is right, why not let us go ahead with it and do something to create a better situation than prevails at the present time? If the policy is wrong why does not the government resign, why does it not go to the country and let the people say whether that policy is a right or wrong one for Canada at the present time?
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are three principal questions, as I look at it, in this country that ought to be settled The first one is the question of population. This has been evidenced by the remarks of probably the best thinking minds and the best financiers in the country. We have had remarks on this subject from men like Sir Henry Thornton, and Mr. Beatty, and from the heads of all our banking institutions, from men who are closely in touch with the financial situation in Canada to-day, and they are unanimous in claiming that the principal problem before the country is to get sufficient population to support the burden that we must carry now and in the succeeding years. The second question is the tariff question on which I intend to speak later. The third question is that of freight rates. These, I believe, are the three principal difficulties which confront Canada at the present time.
First, Sir, let me take up the question of population or immigration. Last year speaking in this House I made a reference to the emigration from Canada to the United States, which at that time I thought was very serious, and I stated that 182,000 of our people had
gone to the adjoining republic during 1923 The Prime Minister replied in these words.
My hon. friend, I presume, knows-
I ask the House to mark those words.
-that the figures he is quoting from the returns of the United States Immigration bureau are not regarded even by the United States government as in any wav corresponding to the true situation; that the census of the United States, for example, is entirely different from the showing made by the immigration statistics.
I pointed out at that time that the figures which I quoted represented the exact number who had paid the head tax upon entering t'he United States. I have no doubt at all that hon. gentlemen opposite did not believe the figures I then gave, but I should like to establish their accuracy now by quoting an even better authority. As reported at page 2014 of Hansard of this year the Minister of Labour quoted these figures regarding the emigration from Canada to the United States for the year 1923-the year for which I gave figures that were disputed' by the Prime Minister:
Immigrant aliens admitted to the United States from Canada during 1923, 182,369.
Or 369 more than I claimed a year ago.
Number of admissions during the year 1924, 159,098.
The minister gave the figures for 1924 as 159,098. Personally I am satisfied that as many Canadians left this country for the United States in 1924 as did in 1923, and this exodus is still continuing. It is quite true that t'he government claim that a certain number of those people are returning; but on that point I want to quote another authority-a gentleman whom I am sure every member of this House knows well and regards with the deepest respelct. This gentleman i.s Mr. C. G. MacNeil, of the Great War Veterans' Association, whose figures are as follows:
During the year ending July 1, 1924, 200,690 persons with Canadian domicile gained admittance to the United States upon announcing intentions of permanent residence in that country. This official tabulation does not include those who left Canada for a temporary stay in the United States, but who eventually* remained.
In this connection I should like to remark that the Minister of Labour stated that many of these people are returning to Canada again and gave figures showing that in 1923, 43.432 returned and in 1924 the number was 43,316. He stated that these figures represented Canadians who had paid the $8 head tax and had obtained a refund on their return to Canada. I am quite sure that the minister, if he thinks t'he matter over in a sober manner and after due reflection, will not repeat that statement in public, because the figures as furnished by
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

the American authorities of those who have actually returned and received a refund of head tax, during the five months beginning with April 1924 are respectively 265, 215, 259, 199 and 190. That is a vastly different story, because those figures constitute less than one-fifth of the number claimed by the Minister of Labour. I have other extracts here on the subject but I have no desire to take up time by reading them. I think I can prove conclusively to the satisfaction of any fair-minded man, either by the statistics of the United States or of Canada that we have lost during the last three years 500,000 population.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh no.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is no question
about it. My hon. friend shakes his head but I ask him if Canadians have not gone to the United States from his own town. I am sure he will not deny it. There is not a member in this House who will say that his constituency has not lost people who have gone to the United States in the last three years. They consist of the very best class of the young active men that we have in this country. Those Canadians who are leaving for the United States comprise many of our skilled workmen; they include young men who have been educated, to a great extent, by the different provinces of the Dominion, and have gone to the United States because they cannot find suitable occupation in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would my hon friend give the official figures of the estimate of the loss of population obtained from the Bureau of Statistics?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have already given the figures for 1923. They were disputed by the Prime Minister when I gave them to the House last j'ear but this session they have been verified by the Minister of Labour.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What figures
does my hon. friend refer to.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figures of those who emigrated to the United States and declared their intention to remain there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I asked my
hon. friend to give an official estimate of the population he said we had lost during the last three years. The Bureau of Statistics makes such estimates, and it is open to my hon. friend to obtain the figures.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is entirely mistaken. I did not say we had lost population; I said we had lost good Canadian citizens which is vastly different.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
" Population "
was the word my hon. friend used.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well we have lost to the United States, in my opinion, 500,000 people in the last three years. I do not care whether the government is expending one dollar or twenty dollars to bring Doukhobors here; I would sooner see Canadians remain in their own country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to ask my hon. friend how it is the cities and towns in Ontario and Quebec have a greater population than they had three years ago according to the municipal returns?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That may be quite true. The unemployed, even in my hon. friend's constituency I have no doubt, flock to the cities. That is the answer.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are making misstatements. .

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quite sure the
answer that I gave was a reasonable one. The trend of the population has been to the United States for many years, as my hon. friend knows, but in hard times unemployment is rife. Every member in this House, whether on this side or the other, knows that the general tendency is to go to the city and look foT relief; and undoubtedly that is the case in the particular instance referred to. I was going to point out, if I could, in a feeble way, what this really meant to Canada. There can be no question that the figures that I have given-and if necessary I will read reports from American authorities which present much larger figures than the ones I am giving-prove that we have lost, largely from Quebec and Ontario but also from the eastern provinces, five hundred thousand young, active men who have gone to the United States. If we take their earning power at only one thousand dollars a year, which is a very low estimate-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon.
member mean that we have lost that number, that the population of Canada has decreased to that extent?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have answered that.
I do not care a cent what the statistics show, but during three years we have lost five

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
hundred thousand people to the United States, and the Department of Immigration of the government of which my hon. friend is a member cannot show one-half of that immigration during the same time that remained in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The population has increased, as shown toy the statistical department, and has been as great during the last three years as at any time during the last decade. Their estimates have been twice verified by the census returns.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That will not be the
case this year. My hon. friend cannot get away from the proposition I put up. We are losing people to the United States. The facts are incontrovertible.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are coming back.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not come back. I made a very low estimate when I said that the earning power of each man was one thousand dollars.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
think if a man could earn one thousand dollars he would go to the States? Would he not stay in this country?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That may be true, but if we had work for them here, they would earn that amount of money in Canada and spend it here. That is the point I am making. My hon. friend will admit that one thousand dollars a year is not too much for a young man to earn.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My estimate then is fair.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If they could earn that amount of money in this country they would not leave. I do not say that they are leaving however.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The very fact that they cannot earn money is the reason they leave Will my hon. friend say that for a skilled workman a thousand dollars a year is an unfair salary?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I would not say that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am saying that it is a fair salary and I am using that figure. If we have been losing five hundred thousand men in the last three years, we have been losing five hundred million dollars of business in this country. If these young men could get work in Canada, what would they do with
their money? They would spend it in Canada. They would have to be housed and clothed and they would require the ordinary necessaries of life. We are losing as long a3 these men remain out of Canada, one thousand dollars per man, and this amounts to many millions per year. I am going to prove that when I come to the tariff, and to show what we have lost by the figures of the government themselves.	'

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How does the hon. member explain that the compensation board of the province of Ontario have paid out in wages for the year 1924 over $9,000,000 more than was paid out in 1921?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think the compensation board has anything to do with it. It just happened there were more men injured than before.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The report states that it has been paid out in wages.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The compensation board
pays no wages.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, but the industries paid $9,000,000 more than they paid in 1921.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That does not make any difference. The hon. gentleman knows, if he comes from Ontario,-and I do not know his constituency-that factories are closing ali around and there are many men out of work all over Ontario on that account. The argument that they paid out more in wages does not signify anything. The other fellows have gone away; that is what I am trying to prove at the present time and the statement of my hon. friend is beside the question. I should like any hon. member who disputes the facts I have given to go to any manufacturing town in Ontario, Quebec, Halifax or any of the eastern provinces, and ascertain the situation. We do not require to be told about it. We all know what it is. I was going to give a few figures in contrast to the five hundred thousand we have lost in the last three years. The present government has more than doubled the expense of the Immigration department of this country in the last few years. I will quote from the Department of Immigration and Colonization of this government, sessional paper No. 13, page 7, and there can be no question about that authority. The statistics are:
1922		 89,999
1923		  72,887
1924		 148,000
In 1923, when we lost 180,000 to the United States, our total immigration was 72,887, and
23SS
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

last year, when we lost 159,000, we got from Europe 148,500.
What is the answer to that? Does the government deliberately desire to have this country populated with men who are flexible in their ideas and exchange our Canadians for them? Or are they trying to keep Canada for Canadians? These are the figures and that is the situation. That is the reason why we are contending that the whole thing is a farce, so far as this government is concerned. The Speech from the Throne left out one other item which would only go to prove the argument I am advancing. Two or three years ago we had a very strenuous situation regarding housing in Canada, and it became so serious that the government was prepared to put up $20,000,000 for a scheme to assist in this regard. Since this government came into power, and especially during the last few years, we have not heard one word about the housing scheme-absolutely nothing. Do hon. members know why? The people have left Canada and they do not require the houses. If we go to the city of Toronto or the city of Hamilton or other large places we can rent houses for a third of the amount asked a few years ago, and have no difficulty in getting houses. That is one thing the government seem to pride themselves on. That is the situation so far as Ontario is concerned.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In Montreal they are
building all the time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have a large industrial situation there and conditions are different. However, this year Ontario may improve in that respect.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is an improvement.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some people think so.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How many new
houses have been built in Ontario cities in the last three years?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Building permits in Toronto alone were 7 per cent less than thev were the year before.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Every city has had an increase in building permits in the last three years.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Except in Montreal there was no increase last year.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In Montreal the
construction has been increased.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I said so-27 per cent
increase in Montreal, 7 per cent decrease in Toronto and all other cities.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How does the hon.
member reconcile that with his statement now?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go on.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) this afternoon made a very pertinent remark, which described the situation as regards the government side most aptly. He said the tariff was a matter of geography. It is absolutely so as regards the government and that has always been the case. During the last election the tariff was simply a matter of geography. The government had just as many policies as there were different sections in the Dominion of Canada, and I believe they still intend to pursue that policy. There i3 one difference that stands out in the mindfe of both my hon. friends opposite and my hon. friends to my left-they have no doubt at all as to the fiscal policy of this small party to their right. We do not change our politics according to geography. We have the same policy from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend believe in an iron-clad policy on this tariff?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not care what
kind of a policy it is so long as it is a policy, but my hon. friends have no policy and they never had one.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend admit their geography is shrinking?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Temporarily, although it
is not decreasing at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Shrinking, I said, getting
smaller.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question as regards
the tariff is: Whom does it benefit? I know my hon. friends to my immediate left will say that the tariff is maintained for the purpose of benefiting the capitalists. They . will all agree to that. I see a lot of them nodding their heads.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
About five per cent of
the population.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, the
man who benefits most from the tariff is not the manufacturer, but the working man and the farmer.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us laugh.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to prove that.

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not the farmers of the west.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The farmers of the west
will one day, we hope, be as prosperous as the farmers of the east and the farmer of the east to-day is not asking for and does not want free trade. The farmer of tihe east is in exactly the same position as the farmer in the United States. What is the man who lives opposite to us across the Montana border asking for? Free trade? Not at all. He wants protection of the highest possible kind and he is getting it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He sees his mistake now,
does he not?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is demanding more.
The principal object in all protection is to preserve the home market and to give the working man in any country an equal chance with the working man with whom he has to compete. There can be no question at all that even in free trade countries they have a tariff, or safeguarding-of-industries laws, or some other means by which to protect their workmen against those countries which have a lower standard of living or depreciated currency. There is no exception in the world.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman state, under the Safeguarding of Industries Act, how much the manufacturers are benefited, or if it gives them a price-fixing power at all?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may be akin to his friend the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey). The other evening when the hon. member for Springfield was addressing the House, I asked him about the Safeguarding of Industries Act in Great Britain. I knew that the act had been abrogated by the late government. I knew and he knew, or he should have known, that a similar and much more stringent measure is being put on the statute books at the present time. He knew and I knew that there is no question that the British are prepared not only to protect themselves and their industries against countries having debased currencies or lower or worse living conditions, but to declare that against all nations, and this in effect makes an absolutely protective tariff. There is no difference in the world, no matter what you call it. Hon. gentlemen are quite as well aware of that fact as I am.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Answer my question.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have answered it, I
think. I should like to give a few illustrations of what the British and we are up against. I. hold in my hand a statement of current wages
in Germany under date of September 1, of last year. While they are given in marks, I will reduce them to dollars and cents. Any hon. gentleman is at liberty to do his own arithmetic if he wants to, but my arithmetic is more accurate than that of an hon. member who preceded me this evening. In Germany, skilled mechanics in the building trades are absolutely at the top of the list, higher than those engaged in chemical, leather, metal, paper or textile industries. In the building industry they receive .66 gold marks as hourly wage, or a weekly wage of 35.64 gold marks. This, at the ordinary basis of 23.82, brings the weekly wages of the most highly paid German mechanic, that is, in the building trades, to the magnificent sum of $8.40 a week, and he is working nine and ten hours a day. I do not care what stand any other hon. gentleman may take in this House: I do not care whether it is the stand my party takes or not; I am absolutely opposed to allowing goods manufactured under those conditions to come into competition with those manufactured by our workmen in Canada. I do not think I will take the time to read the whole list, but I can assure the House that I am quoting now the highest priced mechanic under date of September 1, 1924.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: From what paper is the hon. member reading?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
From a paper issued by the American Department of Labour. I forget the name just at the moment, but I will give it to the hon. gentleman in the morning. Let us take labour conditions in England, and I am quoting now from the official organ of the government, the Statistical Review. That must be right:

These figures are taken from the statistical report submitted by the present government, and the point I make is that it is absolute
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

nonsense for any country, where living conditions are as they are in Canada and as we hope they will continue to be, to try to compete, with labour at these prices, under any free tirade policy or anything approaching free trade. I do not think that our working men should be asked to labour under these conditions, and as a matter of fact I shall never advocate anything of the kind. Although there has been so much debate here on the budget, there is little difference of opinion regarding the tariff except as between hon. gentlemen to my left and the rest of the House. Hon. gentlemen to my left themselves say that the gentlemen immediately opposite, the party in power, are as strongly protectionist as we Conservatives are, and I have not the slightest doubt that I could look into the eyes of many hon. gentlemen opposite me, especially when the House is rather better attended than it is to-night, who are stronger for protection along certain lines than I am myself. For after all we are not a party of high protectionists; we stand for reasonable protection. So that hon. gentlemen opposite belong to exactly the same school as ourselves; they follow the same course as we do and the only real honest opposition to the tariff comes from hon. gentlemen to my left.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why do you not sit together then?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a difference:
we are absolutely candid in our stand.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The other is camouflage?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why are you opposing a protectionist budget?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you call this a protectionist budget?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is it?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is nothing at all; it is merely a standing pat.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would you raise the tariff if you were in power?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly, on some things I would make a fair increase. The hon. gentleman should remember that a few moments ago one of his leaders rebuked my leader because he reduced the tariff in certain directions.-All we want is a fair tariff.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman explain what he means by "fair."
rather the reverse. So long as I can remember, the province of Ontario at least has always had the deepest concern for and interest in the welfare of the western provinces. And I can remember the time when many hon. gentlemen sitting to my left, one of whom is laughing at the present time, were not in this country at all. I remember when that hon. gentleman himself was not here, and it does seem to me, because these gentlemen have certain fiscal views, that that is no reason why they should try to instil into the minds of a certain number of people in the west that eastern Canada is opposed to that part of the country. There is no reason why they should try to give those people the impression that Ontario is a country composed of capitalists and monopolists; for all that sort of thing is absolutely untrue. In the great province of Ontario there are more farmers than there are anywhere else in the Dominion; there are more farmers in that province than in the three western provinces combined. I am sure there is a greater output of agricultural products in Ontario as regards variety than in those provinces. Hon. gentlemen to my left have their own views, and while we are perfectly willing to do anything possible to aid the west, either in the way of freight rates or by the amelioration of conditions, we do not believe, certainly I do not believe, that hon. gentlemen should come asking this or any other government for concessions Which would operate adversely to the majority of the population of eastern Canada.. I say that frankly. I think that the average man in Ontario, whether farmer or manufacturer or labourer, is a protectionist on principle, and the men in the west should have some sympathy for their viewpoint, which is just as honest as the free traders'.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
not admit that the protection now in eastern Canada is a concession from the west?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We had the tariff before
the hon. gentleman came to Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That may be, but that is no reason why you should have it forever.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman and
his friends came to Canada knowing what the policy of the country was; they took up life in the western part of the country knowing the conditions under which they would have to work. And they made their money there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Life is too short. Now, Mr. LEWIS:	But protection is not a law
we have no quarrel with western Canada; of the Medes and Persians.
	j

The, Budget-Mr. Arthurs

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is not much use
arguing with a man who has made up his mind. I would point out that while hon. gentlemen to my left, collectively,-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would call the hon.
gentleman's attention to the fact that all hon. members who sit to his left are not gentlemen.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I tender my most humble apologies to the hon. member for having overlooked her presence.	'

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon. member admit
that the tariff is a concession?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; it is not a concession, it is a necessity, an absolute necessity. I venture to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if you could get a secret vote in the House tomorrow you would not find five hon. members opposed to the tariff. They are all of the same mind with us; they know that it is an absolute necessity, whether they advocate it or not.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A tariff for revenue.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are no!
opposed to the tariff at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member explain what the tariff is? Is it not a tax that someone must pay?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend said that the United States farmers are asking for protection, and he quoted the duty of 42 cents a bushel on wheat. Will he explain why it is that United States wheat is 8 cents a bushel cheaper in the United States market than Canadian wheat in Canada?-which shows it is absolutely impossible to protect the farmers' commodity.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has my hon. friend never told his constituents that the duty raises the price of the article protected? He has repeated that, five or six times in the House to-night. Here is a case where they have a duty on wheat and the price is lower.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If that is true, what is the
value of a tariff as far as the farmer is concerned? The tariff only raises the price so far as industries are concerned.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As a matter of fact i
has nothing to do with it, especially in this case.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If that is so, why are you
arguing for protection in order to give our people work?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That has nothing to do with it. Further I would point this out, that. While the United States are protecting themselves against the farmers of Canada, they are our principal competitors in many of the markets of the world. I may take Great Britain as an instance. In 1923 the United States shipped 31,461,744 cwt. of wheat, while Canada shipped only 28,486,785 cwt. In the matter of flour the situation was somewhat better, we shipped more than did the United States. In the matter of barley last year alone-the year before was worse-the Americans shipped 5,500,000 cwt., and we shipped only 2,900,000 cwt. Then take bacon, last year our neighbours shipped over seven million pounds sterling worth to Great Britain against our five million, while the year be-.
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

fore the figures were eleven million pounds sterling and three million respectively. I am quoting round figures. In spite of the fact that they are preserving their home market for themselves, they are using their surplus production to compete with us in the only open market we have in the world according to my hon. friends to my left.
I might show the effect which the Fordney tariff had on the export of our products to the United States, but it is not a very pleasant task. It was most remarkable. For instance, in 1921 we shipped 1,009,019 pounds of mutton to the United States, last year the figure had dropped to a mere 11,000 pounds. In 1921 we shipped $12,500,000 worth of cattle, last year only $1,100,000 worth. It shows how effectively the American market is being protected against the products of our farmers, and the figures I have already given demonstrate to what an extent their American rivals are competing in the world s markets. They have a double advantage, they have their home market, and in addition they beat us in the markets of the world.
Now let me deal with the reductions in the tariff that were made at the instance of my hon. friends to the left, because I have no doubt that the tariff reductions m agricultural implements were put forward by the government without a good deal pressure from my hon. friends.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, we will say inducement.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor inducement either.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, moral suasion. At any rate, reductions were made.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will accept the responsibility.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This was the result, and I am quoting now the hon. member for saskatoon (Mr. Evans) who, at page 105 of Hansard, said:
In spite of the much-vaunted cut in the tariff last year, the cost of living to-day in the Dominion is quite as high or higher than it was before the paltry change was made. Goods are just as dear for the workers, the cost of production on the farms is just as high.
Surely I am quoting from good authority. Then I must refer to a certain list put upon Hansard last year by my hon. friend from London (Mr. White), which in itself was very valuable. I might point out that although various members have differed with him
[Mr. Arthurs.l
more or less, they all agree that the price of agricultural machinery to-day, in spite of the one or two cuts made by the government, is just as high as it was when they took office, as a matter of fact probably higher.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Come and prove it. The figures mentioned by the hon. member for London have never been questioned. He pointed out that the abolition of the sales tax more than compensated for any single reduction that had since been made. Hon. gentlemen will have an opportunity of trying to prove that these figures are not correct. But they know that they cannot disprove them, they know that his arguments are not to be controverted, and that the only thing that saved the farmers in the west was not the reduction in duty, but the removal of the sales tax-and as a matter of fact they did not get the full benefit of that. But what was the result?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nobody got it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The only person who got any benefit was the manufacturer of agricultural implements. The hon. member for London said that while the buyer of agricultural machinery had received a less tariff reduction than the sales tax amounted to, on the other hand the manufacturer got more for his implements, because he had the sales tax to come and go on, and besides that he was granted certain concessions in the drawback of duty on the goods which went into the manufacture of these various implements.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman account for the closing of the factories that he has been speaking of for the last hour?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am coming to that. I
have personal knowledge of such cases.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the manufacturer got more for his goods why should he close his factory?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have very intimate
knowledge of factories being closed. But the fact remains that what reductions were made were at the expense of the great iron and steel industry of Canada. I do not use the word "great" in the ordinary sense. It was a growing industry, an industry of which we were all proud, and which by all the laws of nature should be a success in Canada, for we have the greatest iron mines in the world, we have unlimited coal resources, we have the men, we have the machinery, but as a matter of fact we are gradually drifting to the position where almost every dollar's worth of our iron is being imported from the United States. I

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
can give a case in point. My home town happened to have the good fortune to possess a smelter. That has been closed. Do you know where the machinery has gone, Mr. Speaker? It was bought by Henry Ford and shipped to the United States.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We had better get Mr. Ford to run the country, I think.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He appears to be getting along fairly well. As a matter of fact the condition is as I have stated it, not only in my home town but in many other towns where the iron industry predominates.
During his speech in this debate the Prime Minister quoted copiously from the Iron Age in order to bolster up the argument that things are not as good in the United States as they might be. I want to quote from the Iron Age, too; I want to give some figures from that publication for the benefit of my hon. friends to my left. They show the number of men employed and the wages paid in the furnaces and steel mills in Canada for the years 1920 and 1924, as follows:
1920	1924
Men employed in furnaces and
mills	
11,874	5.S86In secondary industries	
101,887	69,485Wages paid-furnaces and mills $22,824,520	$7,825,280In secondary industries	$125,680,417	$83,806,802
I do not say that these results are altogether attributable to the reduction in duties made by this government; I do not mean to go that far, because I want to be fair. But the uncertainty facing these people in the matter of duties has led to the laying off of hundreds and thousands of men in the industries affected; and there is no question about the fact that this is one industry which should remain in Canada. I would point out also- and I quote further from the Iron Age- that during the years 1923 and 1924 the production of pig iron in Canada decreased 52 per cent, which goes to prove what I said before. It is also shown that during 1921, thirty plants engaged in the iron and steel industries or their subsidiaries failed; in 1922, seventy-seven; in 1923, eighty-three, and so on. That shows the extent to which this industry has been affected.
I am now going to quote from an authority that will be accepted, I am sure, by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) ; I refer to Premier Armstrong of Nova Scotia. In fact, I suppose it is hardly necessary for the minister to listen to it. as he is no doubt familiar with what the Premier of Nova Scotia has said in this respect. The solution Mr. Armstrong offered when he came to Ottawa to interview the

Prime Minister was this:	First, a revision
of the customs tariff upon iron and steel and their products, in which consideration should be given to the difficulties now hampering the steel works of Nova Scotia, and so on; lower ad valorem duties on semifinished steel; the cutting out of numerous exemptions, and so on. He points out that in his own province the number employed in 1920 in the iron and steel industry was 13,874, while in 1922 it had fallen to 5,000, showing how hard the industry was hit in that province.

Will the
hon. member permit me? It is only fair in making that comparison to say that in 1919-20 the steel industries of Nova Scotia had been working at full capacity owing to the demand for products required during the war.

The war had been over
two years then.

But that
was immediately following the war-a conjunction of circumstances.

That may be true, but
the hon. gentleman will not dispute the fact that there has been depression, nor will he deny that the figures I gave are, in the main, correct; that there is unemployment and that these industries are suffering in his own province.

As a
matter of fact, in the city of Sydney today the industry is working full time.

Just one-the blast
furnace only.
Oh, no.

I have the figures. Now
let me give another illustration of the effect of the want of proper protection or adequate duties.

Before the hon. member
passes from that, would he permit a question? He has been dealing with the possibility of protecting the farmer. Suppose it be possible to get the wheat farmer to accept a tariff of 40 cents a bushel on wheat, would he agree that the farmer should fix his price so as to take advantage of the tariff?
I am quite willing to accept the hon. gentleman's first suggestion. I have no doubt that outside of the wheat farmer every farmer in Canada would jump at protection. So far as the wheat farmer

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
is concerned, I think there ought to be an embargo against wheat going to the United States, so long as they keep the duty on it; I would support that with both hands. We should not let their milling industry get the benefit of our wheat without the payment of duty-because it goes in there free for milling purposes. We should take advantage of the circumstances under which we live. I am going to take that matter up a little later on another question; I want to hurry through. The hon. gentleman will excuse me; I am certainly in favour of doing anything possible to increase the prosperity of our farmers, whether in the west or in the east. Personally I honestly believe that a protective tariff is the best course to pursue.

Well, granting it be so, I am just a little concerned about the application of it. We will leave the wheat farmer out of it. Take the cattle producer; we will suppose there is a high protection on cattle, sufficient to allow the farmer to make cost plus. Would the hon. gentleman be willing to have the cattle growers of this country fix prices so as to take advantage of the tariff?
If the farmer gets a duty on his cattle and can fix a price, why not the manufacturer?
That is what the manufacturer does now. I want to know if the hon. gentleman will agree to have the farmer do it.

Oh, life is too short; I must get through. I will discuss that at any time with my hon. friend; I am not afraid of the argument, but I have certain remarks I want to put on Hansard and the hour is getting late.	-
I want to point out another result of plain, ordinary tariff tinkering. I am well acquainted in the city of Hamilton, and a couple of years ago I saw a splendid manufacturing establishment going up there, built by Libby-Owens for the manufacture of window glass, the only plant of its kind in Canada. These people have been manufacturing for about twenty years in the United States, protected by a high duty. I can remember when as a hardware man I bought my first American glass, twenty years ago, imported into Canada in competition with Belgium. Well, the factory was started at a cost of $2,500,000. The duty was 12J per cent, and I am sure no hon. member would say that was excessive. The duty was reduced by the 
Belgian treaty to lli per cent. But on account of the present position of the Belgian currency and the fact that this government gave no protection to compensate for its depreciation, the duty on this article actually became less than 3 per cent, and the result is that this factory, employing eight or nine hundred men, is closed and the $2,500,000 invested is lying idle.
Is there not a duty as high as 35 per cent on plate glass?

I am referring to ordinary window glass, not plate glass. The hon gentleman should study the tariff. Ordinarily the duty is Hi per cent; he can verify it himself. My hon. friend can verify that later, but the fact is that this factory is closed. It used last year, or the last year of its operation
59.000	tons of good Canadian material, and it exported or shipped from its factory 18,000 tons of product, a total of 77,000 tons. The same factory used 3,000,000 feet of lumber in making cases and I forget how many thousand tons of straw and other materials were used for packing purposes. Taking only the item of freight, it represents a very large amount. When you have 77,000 tons of material it represents, practically, one hundred train loads of thirty-eight cars; my hon. friend can figure out for himself what that means. Who suffered by that and who gained? lliere is not a gentleman in this House who can say that he got his window glass at a rate one-quarter of a cent cheaper last year than before. But here are 800 men out of work, and
77.000	tons of material, the handling of which is lost to Canada. There is a greatly reduced demand for our lumber, for our straw, and other commodities, as a result of the closing up of this factory, and who benefits?
Will the hon. gentleman say why this factory went out of business when it was enjoying 11 per cent protection?

The hon. gentleman will permit me tc correct him; I said nothing of the kind. What I said was there was 11 per cent protection nominally, but on account of the depreciation in Belgium and the competition from that country it amounted to less than 3 per cent. But even if the factory enjoyed 11 per cent protection and yet was obliged to shut down who benefits? The hon. gentleman does not get his glass one cent cheaper.

Why did the factory shut down, 11 per cent protection is quite an advantage?

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

Does the hon. gsnlleman know, or has he given a thought to, the actual conditions? Has he ever thought of the fact that the Oliver Plough Company are moving to the United States; they are no longer going to manufacture their implements in Canada?
The hon. gentleman has treated my. question with contempt. I happen to know why the Libby-Owens factory cannot compete with the rest of the glass makers.

I am not treating the
matter with contempt, quite the reverse. I am giving these results with regret, I am only too sorry to see the damage inflicted upon the industries in this country. There is no question about what the results are; t'he facts speak for themselves. This particular factory is closed, and the price of glass has not been decreased to the Canadian consumer. That is no advantage to this country; nobody in Canada has benefited, it is the Germans and the Belgians who have derived all the profit. If the hon. gentleman wants to legislate for the Belgians let him go ahead; I certainly will not follow him along that line.
Now let me consider for a short time the question of the home market. Eighty-five to ninety per cent of all the products of Canada are consumed in this country. According to American authorities from 97 to 98 per cent of the products of the United States are consumed at home. I am giving figures as quoted by the Economist which I think are fairly correct. In this House a short time ago the hon. gentleman who leads the Progressive party spoke somewhat slightingly of the home market. To what extent are the actions of the hon. gentleman and his followers tending to neglect of the home market? How much are they tending, rather, to cause Canada to send more and more of her goods to foreign countries in the hope of finding a market at all. I want to ask in view of the fact that the United States to-day is the richest country in the world-there can be no doubt about that-and her foreign trade is only two or three per cent of heT total trade did the United States make her wealth at home or abroad? There can be no question of what the answer to that question must be. The United States is making money out of her home market; it is true she is lending money to foreign countries and sending whatever surplus products she may have to the foreign market, but she is making the bulk of her wealth at home; and the sooner we follow the example of the United States the better it will be for us.
Great Britain has taken care to protect herself against cheap labour. I hold in mj hand the proposals of the government regarding the legislation which is to take the place of the Safeguarding of Industries Act. Under the proposed legislation it is possible to impose-and it is probable it will be enacted- a stronger protectionist tariff than Canada has had for many years. As a matter of fact under the Safeguarding of Industries Act they had duties as high as 50 or 60 per cent and those in a so-called free trade country. I should also like to call the attention of my Progressive friends to the fact that there is no country to-day, I think, with a lower tariff than Canada has at the present time. To be correct, almost every civilized country in the world is greatly increasing its tariff. The Irish Free State is putting higher duties on various articles than they ever had before. British India first increased her tariff from 11 to 15 per cent, and on some goods there is an increase in duty from 20 to 30 per cent. No later than last year an increased rate of duty on most iron and steel products was put into force. Australia has increased its tariff four times since the war. To-day it has not only a high tariff but it has brought into force a dumping clause. In addition it can appraise imports at prices corresponding to prices of similar Australian products. In other words the manufacturing selling price in Australia is taken as the dutiable value in that country.
Is Australia's dumping clause worse than the dumping clause in force in Canada at the present time?

We have no dumping
clause unfortunately.
We have not?
No dumping clause worth anything.

Let my hon. friend ask the
customs officials.

We should have one
fifteen times as strong; what we want is a real dumping clause. Look at the way in which the United States applies its dumping clause. Because of the lower freights at which the smelter at the Soo can deliver to Cleveland and other points on the Great Lakes the United States applied its dumping clause against Canada. Just imagine that in comparison with the kind of dumping clause we have.

Does my
hon. friend think that a dumping clause fifteen times as strong as it is at the present
153i
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

time would be in accordance with the moderate tariff he has been telling us he advocates?

I would prohibit dumping altogether; I would have no hall-measures. In Newfoundland there has been a general increase of 5 per cent on practically all imported goods. In South Africa increases of duty were made in 1919, 1921, 1922 and 1923, applicable to almost every line of commerce. In British Guiana the ad valorem duty was increased by one-third in 1920. From tjme to time the rates have been further increased. In 1921 a surtax of from 15 to 30 per cent was imposed; and in 1922 the surtax was increased by another 15 per cent to 25 per cent.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to mean that he would prohibit the entry of all goods into the Canadian market that would enter into competition with our own manufactures?

No, I am not talking
of that at all. There is something wrong with the hon. member's thinking apparatus. We were talking about a dumping clause- not anything else. In British Honduras there was an increase of 33$ per cent.

I suppose,
as he refusas to explain when invited to do so, it would be useless to ask the hon. member what he understands by a dumping clause.

I have here a list of all the countries in Europe, South America and the British Empire, and in every case there has been a decided increase in duties since the war, some of them most remarkable, running as high as 500 or 1,000 per cent. I am not going over them, but I have them here and any hon. member can look at them if he wishes.
I have a few words to say with regard to the freight situation, and' I desire to point out, particularly to my hon. friends to my left, that the one great trouble with almost all Canadian conditions to-day is not the fact that we have too much or too little tariff, but that we have too high freight rates. Without regard to the condition of our tariff at all, we are paying annually to the railways approximately $500,000,000 a year. We paid last year in customs $120,000,000; or in other words we are paying four times as much in freight rates as we paid out under the total customs tariff. A reduction of five per cent on our freight rates, which would not be excessive, would be equal to a twenty per cent reduction in our tariff, which would give our friends to my left fourteen per cent bonus on their agricultural implements com-
ing into Canada. This shows how serious the situation is, and while I do not pretend to be a freight expert, or to have a trained mind along the lines of freight or transportation charges, I cannot for the life of me see why a carload of wheat going to Fort William, to be ground for the use of the people in Fort William, should be charged two or three times as much freight as if that carload came to Fort William, was ground in transit and sent to another country. Those are the conditions. We have them in Ontario. We have got to pay a far greater rate on freight which is sent us than is paid on freight which goes right past our door to a point much further away. I pointed out last year that whereas the Canadian National Railways had fixed a rate of $9 a ton from Drumheller to Toronto or points in Ontario, or an average of $450 per carload, they were drawing crockery from Vancouver to Halifax for $360 a car, a vastly more costly article to transport, a thousand miles longer haul; still they were asking $90 less freight on it than was being paid on coal. I cannot see any justification for that and that is why I say that one of the great problems facing Canada to-day is the freight tariff. We should have some reasonable means of applying a remedy. I can see no reason for the present condition.
One other subject which I do not think has been touched upon so far is the question of pulpwood. Most hon. members have handled it with gloves, or left it alone. We have had during the last couple of years,-and would have had for five or six years more if we had not called them back-a pulpwood commission in Canada inquiring into the question of pulpwood1. Eventually the 'government had to recall them after they started on a world's tour. The cost of that commission was something like seventy-five or eighty thousand dollars. We have their report which is absolutely non-committal. We find that propaganda is being circulated through Canada at the present time both for and against an embargo on pulpwood. The average man I think does not understand the situation. If he did, he would oppose an embargo. I think I understand the situation and I am opposed to an embargo for several reasons, but more particularly because, especially in the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba,-and I believe all the western provinces-we have two classes of pulpwood. We have the ordinary spruce pulpwood and we have a poplar which is increasing in quantity all the time, especially in this province, for which we have little or no

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
market in Canada at the present time. I think somewhere between ten and twenty thousand tons of poplar are used in this province. For that reason, if for no other, 1 would be opposed to an embargo. However,
I am in favour of an export duty. I do not care whether my	views are
altogether in	accord with	the views
of my associates around me os. not, but I state quite frankly and freely that I am opposed to the export of raw material where it is possible to manufacture it in Canada.
I am opposed to the export of asbestos in its raw state, because we control the world's market. I am opposed to the export of unrefined copper or nickel because, in a similar manner, we should be able to control the world's output and the world's price, and the labour and the profit should be conserved for our own people. In an exactly similar manner I would advocate that this government place an export duty upon pulpwood, starting, say, at fifty cents a cord, increasing the duty to a dollar the second year, a dollar and a half the next year and proceeding in that way. The result would be that the settler or owner would not suffer, but would rather benefit, because the Americans would endeavouT to get the pulpwood at the lowest possible price, knowing the duty would be increased the next year. The result would be that on our present export of 1.400,000 cords per year we would have an income of $700,000, which could be used for the general purposes of Canada or for the purpose of preserving our forests both from fire and from the destroying influence of insects, which are perhaps worse than fire. Therefore I think it would be advisable that the government should carefully consider the proposition of placing an export duty on pulpwood. I am in favour, as I said before, of reserving to our own country the other assets which we have.

Suppose you raised
the export duty high enough, would it not amount to the same thing as placing an embargo on pulpwood?

My proposition would
be not to put it so high as to have that effect. The price of pulpwood is a variable one. The Minister of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment (Mr. Beland) told me the other day that in the Eastern Townships they were Pbtaining, I think, $14 and $16 a cord for their ordinary spruce pulpwood. I speak subject to correction but I am quite satisfied there are parts of Ontario, equally accessible
to the Ontario markets, where the price would be probably $10 a cord; so that, as a matter of fact, the addition of fifty cents or a dollar a cord would have very little effect on the export trade. We would have the benefit of the revenue, and there would be the possible inducement to bring the mills from the United States to Canada, if conditions were suitable.

The hon. member spoke
about raising the price from year to year, say from fifty cents to a dollar. I think I got him aright. He said that the Americans, knowing that that price would be raised, would come in and buy. The statement was made to me the other day that the Americans, anticipating an embargo, had already overbought, and that, for that reason, the price of pulpwood was lower to-day. Is that the case?

From my experience I
would say that such a condition is impossible. Export pulpwood as we have it in this province, because it belongs to the owner is a commodity which is produced largely by the farmer in the winter time, with the assistance, possibly, of a few extra hands, and the quantity available in the winter is more or less limited. It is limited by the quantity of help he can secure and weather conditions. If the snow is deep, very little pulpwood can be got out. If conditions are unfavourable, none is got out. Therefore, I do not think any action of our American friends in that regard could have any effect. That is my experience.

Does this pulpwood not deteriorate very rapidly? I am told that it does and that they would not be able to secure a price if they kept it for any length of time, as it would not be of much value in making pulp and paper.

It does not deteriorate at all if it is piled. If you go to one of these pulp mills, you will see where they have immense quantities piled for eight or ten years. Of course, it is peeled. If the bark is left on, it will deteriorate. As regards deterioration in the hands of the farmer, he is never that much ahead. Farmers are largely small operators; they have a few cords here and there; but in the aggregate this amounts to many millions of cords. A farmer is quite able to take care of his own quantity.
At whose expense would the export tax be collected?

That is up to the government.

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
It would mean that the settler producing that pulpwood would receive that much less.

I said at the beginning that I did not think so. I think the anxiety of the American or other person to get the pulpwood would be equivalent to a small increase of fifty cents a cord, and I believe it will be a dollar in a year.
I want to say just a few parting words. What we require to-day is some policy that will build up Canada. Mr. Mayor and Gentlemen:

Welcome an Inspiration.
Your welcome is of itself an inspiration but apart from that one cannot fail to be inspired by the memories of the past when visiting this city. Here, more than three hundred years ago were laid the foundations of the Canada of to-day. If even in later years and since the birth of this Dominion it required faith and courage to persevere in this task transmitted to us by the founders of Confederation, how shall we estimate the faith, the courage and the strong purpose of those who consecrated their energies and their lives to reclaiming for the cause of Christianity and civilization what was then a vast wilderness in this western world. May the soul and purpose of our nation ever be strengthened by the memory of the ideals which inspired the pioneers of Canada when first they undertook the task which now committed to our keeping.
Quebec is thus unique among Canadian cities, in the associations and traditions to which I have alluded. Whatever differences may exist between the policies of political parties in Canada, I am sure they will be found united in the view that the great national ports of this country should be adequately equipped for the purpose which I have stated. Must look well ahead
In approaching a question, one realizes that we must build not for to-day or to-morrow or for ten years hence, and that no proposals can be regarded as adequate unless they are so comprehensive in their character as to permit of proper extension to meet the necessities of the large future.
